Goods other than tobacco and alcohol are free up to a value of EUR 430. For alcohol bought in another EU state, the page gives guide levels: 10 litres of spirit drinks, 20 litres of intermediate products, 90 litres of wine (at most 60 of them sparkling) and 110 litres of beer. They are evidence for own use, not limits.
malta.src: Source read on 22 November 2026: Malta Tax and Customs Administration (mtca.gov.mt), Travellers Allowances on Accompanied Goods from Non-EU or EU Countries.

poland.h: What the Polish Ministry of Finance says about alcohol
p: From outside the EU, the exemption applies from age 17 (not 18): 1 litre of spirits above 22% or 2 litres of drinks up to 22%, plus 4 litres of still wine and 16 litres of beer. It sits alongside the goods allowance of 430 euros by air or sea and 300 euros by land.

From another EU country, own-use limits that do not indicate trade are 10 litres of spirits, 90 litres of wine (60 of it sparkling), 110 litres of beer and 20 litres of intermediate products such as liqueurs. Border-zone residents and workers and vehicle crews get only 0.5 litre of spirits or 0.5 litre of weaker drinks, plus 0.5 litre of wine and 2 litres of beer.
poland.src: Official source read 23 November 2026: Polish Ministry of Finance, podatki.gov.pl, "Towary przywożone przez podróżnych zwolnione z opłat" (published and updated 15 December 2025).
link: Polish Ministry of Finance: goods carried by travellers exempt from charges

portugal.h: What the Portuguese tax authority adds on alcohol
p: The Autoridade Tributária e Aduaneira travellers guide (dated February 2026) sets the allowance for travellers from non-EU countries at 1 litre of spirits or 2 litres of intermediate products (fortified wine, for example), plus 4 litres of still table wine and 16 litres of beer. It says the quantities can be taken as a proportional assortment of these products.

The same guide says travellers under 17 coming from non-EU countries get no allowance for tobacco products or alcoholic drinks. Amounts above the allowance are charged VAT and excise duty. The guide gives separate, higher figures for travellers coming from other EU member states, which this page does not repeat.
portugal.src: Source read 16 November 2026: Autoridade Tributária e Aduaneira (portaldasfinancas.gov.pt), Guia para Viajantes, February 2026 (PDF, in Portuguese).
link: Portuguese Tax and Customs Authority: travellers guide (Guia para Viajantes)

romania.h: What TAROM tells passengers about alcohol in Romania
p: TAROM's customs page says passengers should declare alcoholic beverages above 1 litre when entering or leaving Romania.

The Travel Doc customs page we read earlier allows travellers aged 18 and over from outside the EU 1 litre of drinks above 22% or 2 litres of drinks up to 22%, plus 4 litres of still wine and 16 litres of beer. Neither is the customs authority's page, so confirm with Romanian customs.
romania.src: Unofficial source, read 22 November 2026: TAROM, the Romanian national airline, page "Customs clearance". It is not the customs authority's page, whose site could not be read. The Travel Doc page (infopages.traveldoc.aero) is undated and names no publisher.

spain.h: What the Spanish tax agency adds on alcohol
p: The Agencia Tributaria leaflet for travellers arriving from outside the EU allows 1 litre of alcohol and alcoholic drinks above 22% alcohol by volume (or undenatured ethyl alcohol of 80% or more), or 2 litres of drinks of 22% or less, plus 4 litres of still wine and 16 litres of beer, per person.

The leaflet says travellers under 17 cannot use these allowances. It also warns that the figures are European Union rules, so a traveller going on to another country should check that country’s own limits. The leaflet separately covers tobacco, pets, cash and cultural property.
spain.src: Source read 16 November 2026: Agencia Tributaria (sede.agenciatributaria.gob.es), leaflet for travellers from non-EU countries (PDF, English and Spanish).
link: Spanish Tax Agency: leaflet for travellers from non-EU countries

lebanon.h: What Lebanese Customs says about alcohol
p: The Lebanese Customs traveller's guide allows arriving travellers aged 18 and over up to 2 litres of whisky, champagne, cognac or a similar spirit, or 4 litres of any other drink. Travellers under 18 get no spirits allowance.

Quantities above that pay normal customs duty, either through a traveller's settlement or a customs declaration. The same guide allows 1 litre of eau de cologne and 100 g of perfume, and medicines in the quantity needed for personal use.
lebanon.src: Official source read 23 November 2026: Lebanese Customs Administration, "Traveller's guide" (customs.gov.lb, in Arabic, translated by us; copyright 2019 on the site).

panama.h: Alcohol in Panama: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: We have no card figure for Panama because we found no readable official page for it.

The official page could not be re-opened, and the UK government's travel advice for Panama, which we also read, says nothing about alcohol. So this section applies the general rule most countries follow: alcohol is usually counted in litres by type, spirits, wine and beer, and a traveller who mixes types is held to the combined share. We have no figure for Panama, so ask the Panamanian customs authority before you travel.
panama.src: Official page not re-opened; the UK government (FCDO) advice read on 16 November 2026 does not cover alcohol. Global rule applied, unofficial.

argentina.h: What stands out when you travel to Argentina
p: Argentina's allowances depend on where you arrive from: alcohol is 2 litres from a country that does not border Argentina and 1 litre from a neighbour, and tobacco is 400 cigarettes or 200 from a neighbour. Cash of US$10,000 or more must be declared. Seeds and plants are not permitted, and WHO lists a ban on importing e-cigarettes.

For medicines, Mercosur Resolution 66/2000 asks patients with narcotic or psychotropic medicines to carry a legalised, health-authority-authorised prescription. The dollar amounts in the allowance decree are old, so confirm current figures with ARCA.

australia.h: What stands out when you travel to Australia
p: Australia is strict on small things: adults get 2.25 litres of alcohol duty-free, and going over means duty on all of it, not just the excess. Tobacco is one unopened packet of up to 25 cigarettes (or 25 g of other tobacco) plus one open packet, and under-18s may not bring any. A$10,000 or more in cash must be declared.

Most seeds need a phytosanitary certificate and must meet the conditions in BICON, and vaping goods are allowed only under a small medical exemption (2 vapes, 20 accessories, 200 mL of liquid). Medicines can come in under the traveller's exemption, up to three months' supply, declared to Border Force.

austria.h: What stands out when you travel to Austria
p: Austria applies the EU rules plus its own details: travellers must be 17 or over for the tobacco and alcohol allowances, heated-tobacco sticks fall under the value limit (EUR 430 by air, EUR 300 otherwise) with at most 800 sticks, and EUR 10,000 or more in cash must be declared when entering the EU. Live plants and seeds need a permit, and there is no general vaping ban.
For medicines, the Ministry of Health allows stays of up to 5 days without a certificate for addictive-substance medicines, and 5 to 30 days only with a prescription and no more than 30 days' supply.

bahrain.h: What stands out when you travel to Bahrain
p: Bahrain's allowances are generous but come with an age floor of 18: 3 litres of alcohol plus 12 cans of beer, and 400 cigarettes or heated tobacco sticks or 250 g of tobacco or 400 nicotine pouches, plus 50 cigars and 250 g of pipe tobacco. The exemption does not cover frequent travellers bringing goods in regularly.

There is no limit on cash, but customs or security can ask you to disclose it and prove its source. Plants and vegetable products need an entry permit from the agriculture ministry, and WHO lists no general vaping ban. For controlled medicines, Bahrain's filing to the UN narcotics board allows only 7 days.

belgium.h: What stands out when you travel to Belgium
p: Belgium follows the EU allowances for travellers arriving from outside the EU: 4 litres of still wine and 16 litres of beer plus either 1 litre of spirits or 2 litres of weaker drinks, and 200 cigarettes (or 100 cigarillos, 50 cigars or 250 g of tobacco), with no duty-free tobacco for under-17s. EUR 10,000 or more in cash must be declared on entering or leaving the EU.
Plants and seeds need a permit, WHO lists no general vaping ban, and the Belgian medicines agency requires official proof of prescription for controlled medicines, limited to 3 months of treatment.

brazil.h: What stands out when you travel to Brazil
p: Brazil's baggage exemption is 12 litres of alcohol in total, on top of the arrival Free Shop's own limit, and 10 packs of foreign cigarettes, 25 cigars or cigarillos and 250 g of tobacco. Alcohol and tobacco may not be part of a child's or teenager's baggage. Cash above US$10,000 must be declared through the e-DBV electronic declaration, where plant parts must also be declared.

Anvisa prohibits any import of e-cigarettes, including for personal use and in hand luggage. For medicines, the rule is a quantity that fits your stay and treatment, with a signed prescription if customs asks.

bulgaria.h: What stands out when you travel to Bulgaria
p: Bulgaria follows the EU rules for arrivals from outside the EU: 4 litres of still wine and 16 litres of beer, and for tobacco 200 cigarettes by air but only 40 by land or sea. Under-17s have no tobacco allowance. Cash of €10,000 or more must be declared, and plants and seeds need a permit.

For medicines, Bulgaria's customs FAQ lets foreigners hold narcotic-group medicines for treatment only, up to 30 days' supply, with a document from the prescribing country. WHO lists no general e-cigarette ban, but no traveller limit is published.

cambodia.h: What stands out when you travel to Cambodia
p: Cambodia's two official sources disagree on tobacco: the airports authority gives 200 cigarettes, the tourism ministry 400, so plan on 200. Alcohol is 2 litres, and neither alcohol nor tobacco may be brought by anyone under 18. Declare more than US$10,000 in cash.

WHO lists a ban on importing e-cigarettes, so leave a vape at home. Seeds and soil need a permit and a phytosanitary certificate. We found no source on medicine limits, so carry the prescription and ask the embassy.

canada.h: What stands out when you travel to Canada
p: Canada's duty-free choice is one of 1.5 litres of wine, 1.14 litres of spirits or 8.5 litres of beer, and 200 cigarettes, 50 cigars or 200 g of tobacco, with the drinking age of the province where you arrive. Declare C$10,000 or more to the CBSA, and declare all plants and seeds.

Vaping is allowed: up to 12 containers of at most 120 ml each for visitors 18 and over. Health Canada lets you carry a 90-day supply of controlled medicines such as amphetamines in the original container, and pseudoephedrine up to 3 g in total.

chile.h: What stands out when you travel to Chile
p: Chile allows 2.5 litres of alcohol or 400 cigarettes, 50 cigars and 500 g of pipe tobacco, both for travellers over 18. Cash above US$10,000 must be declared. The SAG sworn declaration for plants, seeds and soil is filled in online up to a day before arrival.

Chile's ISP has no special health rule for traveller medicines: bring a dated prescription or doctor's certificate not older than 6 months, with the daily dose, in the original packaging. WHO lists no general e-cigarette ban, but no traveller limit is published.

china.h: What stands out when you travel to China
p: China uses a red channel instead of a flat allowance: declare 1,500 ml or more of drinks at 12% alcohol or above, 400 or more cigarettes, or 100 or more cigars. Cash of RMB 20,000 or US$5,000 in foreign currency must be declared, and customs bans fruit, solanaceous vegetables and soil.

For medicines, Shanghai Customs asks you to declare controlled medicine and carry a prescription or diagnosis certificate in a reasonable personal quantity. Officers decide on site. WHO lists no general e-cigarette ban, but no traveller limit is published.

colombia.h: What stands out when you travel to Colombia
p: Colombia sets no litre or cigarette limit. Instead, accompanied baggage worth up to US$2,000 is free of the single tax, and duty-free purchases count towards it. After five days abroad you may bring up to US$3,000 by paying the tax. Declare cash above US$10,000 on Form 530.

Plant products need the phytosanitary certificate of their country of origin. Medicines on the 1961 and 1971 Convention lists may be carried as a standard 30-day treatment with a copy of the prescription. WHO lists no general e-cigarette ban.

croatia.h: What stands out when you travel to Croatia
p: Croatia applies the EU arrival limits (4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer, 200 cigarettes by air but 40 by land or sea) and asks you to declare €10,000 or more in cash. Plants and seeds need a permit.

Its medicine rule is unusually short: the Customs Administration allows medicine containing narcotics for personal use for up to 5 days, with copies of prescriptions or a physician's certificate. WHO lists no general e-cigarette ban.

Croatia's customs pages split tobacco by transport: 200 cigarettes arriving by air or sea from a third country, 40 by road or rail, plus 10 ml of e-liquid and 50 g of heated tobacco. Cash of EUR 10,000 or more is declared on form HR1 or EN1. Seeds and plants for planting must be shown at one of seven border inspection posts, including Zagreb airport and the ports of Ploče and Rijeka.

cuba.h: What stands out when you travel to Cuba
p: Cuba's tourism portal lists 2.5 litres of alcohol and 400 cigarettes, 500 g of pipe tobacco and 50 Cuban cigars per adult. The Customs Declaration for Passengers must always be filled in, and cash above US$5,000 goes on it. You may take out up to US$5,000 freely.

Cuban Customs prohibits plants, seeds, fresh fruit and vegetables and any soil. Controlled medicines need a prescription, a certificate endorsed by your home health authority and one from Cuban health authorities, for up to 30 days.

cyprus.h: What stands out when you travel to Cyprus
p: Cyprus follows the EU limits for arrivals from outside the EU: 4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer and 200 cigarettes. Declare €10,000 or more in cash, and do not bring plants or seeds without a permit.

For medicines, Cyprus's Pharmaceutical Services say visitors carrying small quantities of internationally controlled medicines need a permit from the Inspection Department, with the form on the ministry's website. WHO lists no general e-cigarette ban.

czechia.h: What stands out when you travel to Czechia
p: Czechia uses the EU arrival limits (4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer, 200 cigarettes) and needs a declaration of €10,000 or more in cash. Plants and seeds need a permit.

Its customs page says importing addictive substances needs an import permit from the Ministry of Health, plus an export permit from the origin country where required, with exemptions in Act 167/1998. WHO lists no general e-cigarette ban.

denmark.h: What stands out when you travel to Denmark
p: Denmark applies the EU limits for arrivals from outside the EU: 4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer and 200 cigarettes, with no tobacco allowance under 17. Declare €10,000 or more in cash, and bring no plants or seeds without a permit.

The Danish Medicines Agency allows euphoriant medicines from lists B to E up to a 30-day personal supply, but private persons may not bring list A substances. Its contact is dkma@dkma.dk. WHO lists no general e-cigarette ban.

dominican-republic.h: What stands out when you travel to the Dominican Republic
p: The Dominican Republic allows adults 5 litres of alcohol, and 20 packs of cigarettes, 25 cigars or 200 g of tobacco duty-free. Declare US$10,000 or more on the customs form and be ready to show where the money comes from.

The Agriculture Ministry says airport technicians seize and incinerate fruit and unregistered plant products. The Manual del Viajero lets you carry medicines for personal use with no stated limit, but controlled ones need the prescription justifying their use.

costa-rica.h: What stands out when you travel to Costa Rica
p: Costa Rica allows each adult 5 litres of wine, spirits or liquor and 500 g of processed tobacco duty-free. Declare cash of US$10,000 or more, or securities of US$50,000 or more. The SFE lists seeds, fruit, plants, cuttings and tubers as plant items, and material that enters without the legal procedures is held or destroyed.

The Drug Surveillance Board lets treated travellers bring one month of treatment, with an ID copy, the prescription and a clinical summary issued within three months, all translated into Spanish. WHO lists no general e-cigarette ban.

egypt.h: What stands out when you travel to Egypt
p: Egypt's tourist allowance is 1 litre of spirits and 200 cigarettes, 25 cigars or 200 g of tobacco, with the quantity recorded in your passport. Foreign currency above US$10,000 must be declared, while Egyptian pounds are capped at 5,000. Cairo Airport prohibits any seeds or agricultural seedlings.
Egypt's customs regulations list medicine for personal use as duty-free luggage at the discretion of the control authority, with no quantity or document list. WHO lists no general e-cigarette ban.

estonia.h: What stands out when you travel to Estonia
p: Estonia applies the lower EU tobacco limit to every traveller from outside the EU, even by air: 40 cigarettes, 20 cigarillos, 10 cigars or 50 g. The alcohol limits are the usual EU ones, and €10,000 or more in cash must be declared.

Narcotic or psychotropic medicine may come in without a permit as one retail package of up to 30 units or 25 ml, with a doctor's notice or prescription copy. More, up to 30 days, needs State Agency of Medicines authorisation.

ethiopia.h: What stands out when you travel to Ethiopia
p: Ethiopia's Directive 923/2014 allows 2 litres of alcohol, 200 g of cigarettes and 250 g of loose tobacco for personal use, but WHO lists a ban on importing e-cigarettes. Travellers may carry 3,000 birr, and foreign currency above US$10,000 needs a customs declaration.

Plant quarantine rules need an import permit and phytosanitary certificate for fresh produce and many plants, and soil is banned. Under the EFDA guideline, personal medicine needs no pre-import permit, but port staff check quantity against your prescription.

fiji.h: What stands out when you travel to Fiji
p: Fiji allows 3 litres of spirits, 4.5 litres of wine or 4.5 litres of beer, and 200 cigarettes or 200 g of cigars or tobacco, for travellers 18 and over. Chewing tobacco is prohibited. Declare FJ$10,000 or more on the Border Currency Reporting Form.
BAF treats the arrival card as a legal document, so declare plants and seeds. For medicine, Fiji's guideline asks you to show at the border that it was legally prescribed and supplied to you.

finland.h: What stands out when you travel to Finland
p: Finland follows the EU limits (4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer, 200 cigarettes) and the €10,000 cash declaration. Plants and seeds need a permit.

Its medicine rule depends on where you travel from: Finland counts psychotropic and central nervous system medicines as narcotics, allowing up to 30 days' supply from a Schengen country but only 14 days' from outside it. A pharmacy Schengen certificate is needed inside the Schengen area.

france.h: What stands out when you travel to France
p: France uses the EU arrival limits (4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer, 200 cigarettes) and asks you to declare €10,000 or more in cash. Plants and seeds need a permit.

For medicines, the ANSM says no transport attestation is required and it does not issue one. The original prescription is mandatory, ideally with an English translation if you travel on. WHO lists no general e-cigarette ban.

French customs lets you split the tobacco and alcohol allowances proportionally, so using half of one leaves half of another. Under-17s get no duty-free tobacco or alcohol. Cash of EUR 10,000 or more is declared online through the DALIA service, up to 30 days before the trip. A phytosanitary certificate is needed from the first plant specimen, and soil, grapevines and citrus plants are prohibited.

georgia.h: What stands out when you travel to Georgia
p: Georgia's Revenue Service gives one of 1 litre of drinks at 22% or more, 2 litres under 22%, or 4 litres of wine and 16 litres of beer, and 200 cigarettes, 50 cigars or 250 g of other tobacco, from age 18. At land and sea crossings these are per 30 calendar days. Declare cash above GEL 30,000.

Plants need a permit or certificate. Georgia's customs brochure names methamphetamine and treats ephedrine and pseudoephedrine preparations as controlled, so medicine needs documents, including an English prescription copy approved by your home authority.

germany.h: What stands out when you travel to Germany
p: Germany applies the EU limits and a €10,000 cash declaration, with penalties for an incorrect declaration. Plants, plant products and cut flowers from outside the EU are prohibited without a phytosanitary certificate, except fruit of pineapple, coconut, durian, banana or date.

BfArM's travel page covers narcotics under the Schengen rule: a certificate under Article 75, completed by your doctor and authenticated by the health authority before the trip. It says nothing about ADHD medicines or pseudoephedrine.

greece.h: What stands out when you travel to Greece
p: Greece has the EU's two-level tobacco rule: 200 cigarettes by air but 40 by land or sea. Alcohol follows the EU limits, and €10,000 or more in cash must be declared, with penalties for an incorrect declaration. Plants and plant products need a phytosanitary certificate, except fruit of pineapple, coconut, durian, banana or date.
Medicine rules rely on the Schengen decision: a certificate from the national authority, valid at most 30 days and for one drug each, for residents of a Schengen state.

hong-kong.h: What stands out when you travel to Hong Kong
p: Hong Kong has one of the smallest allowances here: 1 litre of liquor above 30% and 19 cigarettes, 1 cigar or 25 g of tobacco, for travellers 18 and over. Its Department of Health says incoming travellers may not bring e-cigarettes or heated tobacco, and any carried must be declared. Declare more than HK$120,000, with fines up to HK$500,000.
The Drug Office treats amphetamine as a dangerous drug: even a visitor in transit needs written approval before arrival, processed in about 10 working days. Plants need a licence and a certificate.

hungary.h: What stands out when you travel to Hungary
p: Hungary follows the EU limits, with 200 cigarettes by air and 40 by land or sea, and a €10,000 cash declaration. Plants from outside the EU need a phytosanitary certificate, except fruit of pineapple, coconut, durian, banana or date.

Its medicine rule is tiered by length: for narcotic drugs, up to 3 days needs only a GP's international certificate and 3 to 90 days an official certificate; for psychotropics, up to 30 days with a GP certificate. You show documents at the customs and police check.

iceland.h: What stands out when you travel to Iceland
p: Iceland counts alcohol in units (for example 1 litre of spirits plus 0.75 litre of wine plus 3 litres of beer) and sets the age at 20, while tobacco is 200 cigarettes from age 18. Vaping is allowed duty-free up to 40 ml of e-liquid or 20 disposable vapes. Declare more than €10,000.
Up to 25 cut flowers and 2 kg of bulbs travel free. The Medicines Agency allows 30 days' supply of narcotic or psychotropic medicine from outside the EEA, measured in defined daily doses.

india.h: What stands out when you travel to India
p: India's duty-free allowance is 2 litres of alcohol and 100 cigarettes, 25 cigars or 125 g of tobacco, and imported tobacco must carry India's pictorial health warning. Its 2019 Act bans importing e-cigarettes, including heat-not-burn products. Declare foreign currency over US$5,000 in notes, or US$10,000 in total.

The customs guide lists narcotic and psychotropic substances as prohibited imports and plants and their produce as restricted, so a prescription alone is not safe to rely on. Ask Indian customs first.

indonesia.h: What stands out when you travel to Indonesia
p: Indonesia allows adults 21 and over 1 litre of alcohol, and 200 cigarettes, 25 cigars or 100 g of cut tobacco. E-cigarettes have their own limits for ages 18 and over: 140 solid sticks or 40 capsules, 30 ml of open-system liquid or 12 ml of closed-system liquid. Anything over a limit is destroyed on the spot.
Plants need a phytosanitary certificate, and seeds an import permit. BPOM's leaflet bars narcotic medicines from passenger bags, while psychotropic medicines need a prescription, up to 60 days.

ireland.h: What stands out when you travel to Ireland
p: Ireland follows the EU limits for arrivals from outside the EU (4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer, 200 cigarettes) and the €10,000 cash declaration. Plants and plant products need a phytosanitary certificate, except fruit of pineapple, coconut, durian, banana or date.

The Department of Health asks visitors from a Schengen country for an Article 75 certificate when a medicine contains a controlled drug in Schedule II or III of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2017, valid up to 30 days and covering one drug.

Irish Revenue lets you split the spirits and weaker-drink allowances, for example 0.5 litre of spirits with 1 litre of port, and the tobacco allowance fractionally. Oral smokeless tobacco is generally prohibited. Customs can seize cash of EUR 1,000 or more it suspects is linked to crime, apart from the EUR 10,000 declaration. Plants are checked by the Department of Agriculture at Dublin Port, Dublin Airport and Rosslare Europort.

israel.h: What stands out when you travel to Israel
p: Israel's duty-free allowance for entrants 18 and over is 1 litre of spirits and 2 litres of wine, and tobacco up to 250 g or 200 cigarettes. The green channel counts as your declaration that you carry only permitted items. Report NIS 50,000 or more, or NIS 12,000 when entering or leaving Gaza.

Plants and seeds need a Ministry of Agriculture licence before you arrive. The Ministry of Health's 90-day allowance for personal medicines excludes narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, which follow different rules.

italy.h: What stands out when you travel to Italy
p: Italy applies the EU limits for arrivals from outside the EU (4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer, 200 cigarettes) and the €10,000 cash declaration, with penalties for an incorrect declaration. Plants need a phytosanitary certificate, except fruit of pineapple, coconut, durian, banana or date.

Italy exempts carried medicines from specific requirements, except those with narcotic or psychotropic substances. Travellers from Schengen countries need an Article 75 certificate valid 30 days, issued on a doctor's prescription.

Italy's customs agency counts each allowance as 100%, so any mix of tobacco or alcohol is fine if the shares add up to no more than 100%. Goods above the allowance can be left in customs custody for 90 days while formalities are completed. Cash of EUR 10,000 or more is declared at a customs office. Plant foods for personal use that need no certificate are capped at 5 kg fresh or 2 kg dried.

jamaica.h: What stands out when you travel to Jamaica
p: Jamaica allows passengers 18 and over 2 litres of alcohol, and 200 cigarettes, 50 cigars or 230 g of processed tobacco. Form C5 asks whether you carry currency worth more than US$10,000. Plants need a permit, and amnesty bins at Kingston and Montego Bay airports let you hand items in.
For prescription drugs, the foreign ministry page asks for a special permit, applied for with a physician's letter, a prescription copy and flight details.

japan.h: What stands out when you travel to Japan
p: Japan's duty-free allowance is 3 bottles of about 760 ml each, and 200 cigarettes, 50 cigars, 10 packages of heat-not-burn tobacco or 250 g of other tobacco. Other goods are exempt up to ¥200,000 in total, and a single item above that pays duty on its full value. Declare more than ¥1,000,000. Plants need a certificate and inspection, and soil is prohibited.

Japan's health ministry treats amphetamine, the ingredient in Adderall, as prohibited for individual travellers, even with a foreign prescription. Sudafed's pseudoephedrine is listed with stimulant raw materials.

jordan.h: What stands out when you travel to Jordan
p: Queen Alia airport's guide gives each passenger 18 and over a bottle of spirits up to 1 litre and 200 cigarettes. Cash above JOD 10,000 must be declared under the Anti-Money Laundering Law of 2021. WHO lists a ban on importing e-cigarettes.

We found no source specific to Jordan on plants and seeds, so that card shows the general rules. For medicines, a regulation filed with the INCB covers narcotics and psychotropics together: personal use only, no more than six months.

kenya.h: What stands out when you travel to Kenya
p: Kenya asks you to declare, not just stay within limits: spirits over 1 litre, wine over 2 litres, tobacco over 250 g, perfumes over a litre in total, and currency worth US$10,000 or more. KRA lists plants and plant material as restricted.
Kenya's filing to the UN narcotics board allows 30 days for both narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, with a valid prescription and the original packaging.

kuwait.h: What stands out when you travel to Kuwait
p: Kuwait is one of the few countries here where alcohol is illegal to import, and failing to declare can mean imprisonment, refusal of entry and deportation. Tobacco falls in a duty exemption of 3,000 Saudi riyals in goods, with no more than 400 cigarettes. Declare 3,000 dinars or more in cash.

Under the GCC plant quarantine law, travellers' plants are inspected and anything for planting is excluded. Kuwait's INCB filing allows only schedule 2, 3 and 4 substances and says narcotic drugs are currently not allowed at all.

latvia.h: What stands out when you travel to Latvia
p: Latvia follows the EU limits: 200 cigarettes by air but 40 by land or sea, with the usual alcohol limits and a €10,000 cash declaration. Plants need a phytosanitary certificate, except fruit of pineapple, coconut, durian, banana or date.

For medicines with Schedule II or III substances entering from a Schengen country, the State Agency of Medicines requires a certificate from the authority of the country you come from. From outside Schengen, up to 14 days needs no permit.

lebanon.h: What stands out when you travel to Lebanon
p: Lebanese Customs allows arriving adults 800 cigarettes, 2 litres of spirits or 4 litres of other drinks, and asks for a declaration of cash above 15,000 US dollars, not 10,000. The Beirut airport website also says arriving passengers may not carry fresh fruit and vegetables. WHO lists no general e-cigarette ban.

Lebanon's filing with the UN narcotics board allows 7 days of narcotic drugs and 30 days of psychotropic substances, so the class of the drug decides how much you may bring. The filing also needs approval of the Department of Narcotics.

lithuania.h: What stands out when you travel to Lithuania
p: Lithuania follows the EU limits: 200 cigarettes by air but 40 by land or sea, the usual alcohol limits and a €10,000 cash declaration. Plants need a phytosanitary certificate, except fruit of pineapple, coconut, durian, banana or date.

Its customs page names examples of narcotic medicines (buprenorphine, fentanyl, methadone, morphine, pethidine, tramadol) and psychotropic ones (alprazolam, diazepam, clonazepam, lorazepam, zolpidem, phenobarbital, higher-dose codeine). Adderall is not among them.

luxembourg.h: What stands out when you travel to Luxembourg
p: Luxembourg applies the EU limits for arrivals from outside the EU (4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer, 200 cigarettes) and the €10,000 cash declaration. Plants and plant products need a phytosanitary certificate.

Its filing to the UN narcotics board asks for a copy of the valid prescription and a doctor's certificate endorsed by your home health authority, and says the Schengen agreement applies. It gives no day or quantity limit.

The Luxembourg government portal Guichet.lu adds: between EU countries there is no limit on personal purchases, but amounts above 800 cigarettes, 400 cigarillos, 200 cigars or 1 kg of smoking tobacco, 10 litres of spirits, 20 litres of intermediate drinks, 90 litres of wine (60 sparkling) or 110 litres of beer are presumed commercial and excise becomes due. From outside the EU you must declare your goods at the customs office. Items bought on a trip that make up one multi-part set count as one item, whatever the number of invoices. Human medicines are banned unless they cover your own needs, and fuel is limited to the standard tank plus a 10-litre can. The portal page was last changed on 11 June 2018 and says it is being updated.
luxembourg.src: Official source read 23 November 2026: Guichet.lu, Government of Luxembourg, "Importation de marchandises vers le Luxembourg" (in French, translated by us; last modified 11 June 2018).

malaysia.h: What stands out when you travel to Malaysia
p: Malaysia allows 1 litre of alcohol in all, but lists no duty-free tobacco amount: the declaration form asks everyone whether they carry tobacco, and failing to declare dutiable goods is an offence. Declare more than US$10,000, and do not bring ringgit worth more than that without Bank Negara approval. WHO lists a ban on sale of e-cigarettes, but no import ban.
Seeds and cuttings need a MAQIS permit and a phytosanitary certificate. Prescription medicines with dangerous drugs must be declared, with a prescription or doctor's letter in English.

maldives.h: What stands out when you travel to Maldives
p: The Maldives bans importing alcohol under Law No. 4/1975 and Customs advises not to buy it on the flight or in duty-free shops, as it is confiscated at the airport. Tourists 18 and over may bring 200 cigarettes, 25 cigars or 250 g of tobacco, and held goods can be collected at departure. Report US$10,000 or more.

All plants need a phytosanitary certificate and inspection. Customs lists narcotics and psychotropics as prohibited but also asks for a registered doctor's prescription for controlled drugs, so the position needs checking.

malta.h: What stands out when you travel to Malta
p: Malta follows the EU limits for arrivals from outside the EU (4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer, 200 cigarettes) and the €10,000 cash declaration. Plants need a phytosanitary certificate, except fruit of pineapple, coconut, durian, banana or date.
Malta's filing to the UN narcotics board, dated 3 January 2017, asks only for a valid medical prescription and says the Schengen agreement applies. It states no day or quantity limit.

Malta International Airport's customs page (the airport operator, repeating the customs rules) says arrivals from outside the EU use the green channel only if they carry no more cash or excise goods than allowed and no prohibited or restricted items; otherwise, or if in doubt, use the red channel. It lists as prohibited or restricted: smokeless tobacco (chewing tobacco, heets, snus, snuff), unbranded tobacco, flavoured tobacco, narcotics, protected animals, birds and bird skins, live plants and plant products, live animals, counterfeits, weapons and high-value items. Meat and dairy from outside the EU must be declared or you risk a fine, prosecution and confiscation; small personal amounts are allowed from the Faroe Islands and Greenland, and there is no limit from EU countries, Andorra, Iceland, Northern Ireland, Liechtenstein, Norway, San Marino and Switzerland.
malta.src: Source read 23 November 2026: Malta International Airport, "Customs" page (maltairport.com). It is the airport operator, not the customs authority, whose own site was timing out.

mauritius.h: What stands out when you travel to Mauritius
p: Mauritius gives adults 18 and over a choice of three alcohol options (for example 1 litre of spirits plus 2 litres of wine or beer), each with 250 g of tobacco, under a table that has applied since 1 September 2025. The MRA lists vapes, e-liquid and heated tobacco as prohibited goods. Use the red channel above Rs 500,000.

Plants, seeds, cut flowers, fruit and soil need Ministry clearance. For controlled medicines you need approval from the Government Pharmacist, a legible prescription and the original containers, for one month.

mexico.h: What stands out when you travel to Mexico
p: Mexico allows adults 18 and over up to 3 litres of alcoholic drinks and 6 litres of wine, and 20 packs of cigarettes, 25 cigars or 200 g of tobacco, and the separate US$500 goods allowance cannot be used for them. ANAM lists e-cigarettes and vaporisers as merchandise you cannot bring in. Not declaring cash above US$10,000 is fined 20% to 40% of the excess.
SENASICA regulates seeds, bulbs, cuttings and plants, and prohibits soil, straw, hay and palm. For psychotropic substances you must show the corresponding prescription.

morocco.h: What stands out when you travel to Morocco
p: Morocco's customs guide gives visitors one 1-litre bottle of wine and one of spirits, and 200 grams of manufactured tobacco, without declaration. Declare 100,000 dirhams or more and keep the endorsed form, which proves the origin of the money when you leave. Plant products need an ONSSA phytosanitary certificate.

Morocco's filing to the UN narcotics board sets no day limit for controlled medicines but asks for more paper than most countries: a prescription, a patient's written request, and for a medicine not sold in Morocco an authorisation.

nepal.h: What stands out when you travel to Nepal
p: Nepal gives a foreign passenger one bottle of up to 1 litre of liquor or up to twelve cans of beer, not both, and 200 cigarettes, 50 cigars or 250 g of tobacco. WHO lists a ban on importing e-cigarettes. Declare more than US$5,000 in cash.

Plants, soil and moss need an advance entry permit and a phytosanitary certificate, presented at the quarantine office before customs. We found no source on medicine limits for Nepal, so that card gives none.

netherlands.h: What stands out when you travel to the Netherlands
p: The Netherlands applies the EU limits for arrivals from outside the EU (4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer, 200 cigarettes) and the €10,000 cash declaration. Plants and seeds need a permit.

The Dutch government says ADHD medication falls under the Opium Act, List I, which names active ingredients, not brands. Opium Act medicines can enter only with an official statement, so check whether amphetamine is on the list.

new-zealand.h: What stands out when you travel to New Zealand
p: New Zealand allows 4.5 litres of wine or beer or 3 bottles of spirits (age 17 and over), and 50 cigarettes or 50 g of tobacco, the lowest cigarette figure among these hubs. Other goods are exempt up to NZ$700. Report NZ$10,000 or more on a Border Cash Report, online within 72 hours of travel.

Seeds, bulbs, flowers and soil are biosecurity risk goods: declare them or risk an NZD 400 fine. Medsafe allows three months of a non-controlled prescription medicine and one month of a controlled drug, and the Ministry of Health says pseudoephedrine medicines are controlled.

nigeria.h: What stands out when you travel to Nigeria
p: Nigeria's passenger concessions list one 1-litre bottle of spirit, one 1-litre bottle of wine and 200 grams of tobacco, and choosing the green or red exit counts as your declaration. A customs notice from 2016 sets a US$10,000 cash threshold, so confirm the current figure. The UK government says importing fruit, vegetables and cereals is illegal.
We found no official source on Nigerian medicine limits, so that card states none; carry the prescription in its original packaging and ask NAFDAC.

norway.h: What stands out when you travel to Norway
p: Norway sets age limits of 18 for beer and wine and 20 for drinks over 22%, bans drinks over 60%, and gives visitors 200 cigarettes or 250 g of tobacco. Since 1 January 2026 private individuals may not import nicotine vapes or e-liquid. Notify customs of currency above NOK 25,000 or risk a fine of 20% of the amount.

For narcotic medicines, NOMA wants them prescribed for you, documented and declared in the red zone; without a Norwegian address you may bring up to 30 days' use with a prescription copy or doctor's letter.

oman.h: What stands out when you travel to Oman
p: Oman allows only non-Muslims alcohol, up to 2 litres of wine and 48 cans of beer, and gives up to 400 cigarettes, neither for frequent border crossers. WHO lists a ban on importing e-cigarettes. Declare OMR 6,000 or more, and the green or red channel also counts as your declaration.

Seeds and live plants need a phytosanitary certificate, untreated soil is banned and fines go up to OMR 1,000. Oman's filing to the UN narcotics board gives the same 30-day limit for narcotic and psychotropic drugs.

panama.h: What stands out when you travel to Panama
p: For Panama we found no source on alcohol or tobacco limits, so those cards show general rules and say so. Tourism Panama says you declare only cash, objects or documents worth more than US$10,000, with an online traveller's affidavit and a QR code. Tocumen airport requires a phytosanitary certificate for every live plant and plant product.
Panama's filing to the UN narcotics board allows up to 90 days for either narcotic or psychotropic medicines, with a valid prescription and a doctor's certificate.

peru.h: What stands out when you travel to Peru
p: Peru allows 3 litres of liquor and 20 packs of cigarettes, 50 cigars or 250 g of tobacco, for travellers over 18. SUNAT lists cash up to US$10,000 as exempt baggage, and omitting or falsifying a declaration leads to a 30% penalty on the undeclared value. Only dried products up to 1 kg may come as plant items, and soil is not allowed.
Peru's filing to the UN narcotics board allows narcotic drugs for up to 5 days only, while psychotropic substances may be carried in the amount of the prescription.

philippines.h: What stands out when you travel to the Philippines
p: The Philippines gives 2 bottles of liquor with a total value of P10,000 or less, and 2 reams of cigarettes, 50 cigars or 250 g of pipe tobacco, free of duty and tax. Declare foreign currency above US$10,000. Live plants need an international phytosanitary certificate and an SPSIC from the Bureau of Plant Industry, or they can be seized.
A 2015 joint circular of the DOH, FDA and Customs puts dangerous drugs and controlled precursors under the Dangerous Drugs Board and gives no traveller allowance.

poland.h: What stands out when you travel to Poland
p: Poland follows the EU limits: 200 cigarettes by air but 40 by land or sea, the usual alcohol limits and a €10,000 cash declaration. Plants and seeds need a permit.

Poland's Chief Pharmaceutical Inspectorate asks for a document before you carry any medicine on its list of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, issued within 15 days before you cross the border.

Poland's duty-free exemption for tobacco and alcohol starts at age 17, not 18. Border-zone residents and workers and vehicle crews have their own, lower limits. Between Schengen countries cash need not be declared, but crossing the Schengen border with EUR 10,000 or more must be. For plants, Poland's inspectorate separates plants not for planting, which may enter at any crossing, from seeds and planting material, which need a designated inspection post and a TRACES NT notification.

portugal.h: What stands out when you travel to Portugal
p: Portugal applies the EU limits for arrivals from outside the EU (4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer, 200 cigarettes) and the €10,000 cash declaration. Plants and seeds need a permit.

Decree-Law 15/93, Article 13, published by Infarmed, lets people crossing the border carry controlled substances for their own use, up to 30 days of treatment, with a medical document justifying the need.

Portugal's tax authority guide of February 2026 allows 200 cigarettes, 1 litre of spirits or 2 litres of intermediate products such as fortified wine, and gives separate allowances for heated tobacco, e-liquid and nicotine pouches. Travellers under 17 get no tobacco or alcohol allowance. Cash of EUR 10,000 or more, including gold since June 2021, is declared through the customs portal. The food and veterinary authority warns that plants for planting carry a high pest risk.

qatar.h: What stands out when you travel to Qatar
p: Hamad International Airport lists alcohol among items that cannot be imported under any condition, and it is confiscated at arrival screening. Tobacco is allowed up to 400 cigarettes or 2 kg of shisha tobacco, worth no more than QAR 3,000. WHO lists a ban on importing e-cigarettes. Declare QAR 50,000 or more.

Poppy and hemp seeds are forbidden, and live plants and cut flowers need approval. For controlled medicines the Ministry of Public Health requires a permit through its electronic system, approved or rejected within three working days.

romania.h: What stands out when you travel to Romania
p: Romania applies the lower EU tobacco limit to every traveller from outside the EU, even by air: 40 cigarettes, 20 cigarillos, 10 cigars or 50 g. Alcohol follows the usual EU limits, and €10,000 or more in cash must be declared.

Romanian Customs says that when you enter from a non-EU state you must declare in writing, in every case, medicines containing narcotic or psychotropic substances, and a wrong or missing declaration can be fined.

russia.h: What stands out when you travel to Russia
p: Russia applies Eurasian Economic Union norms: 3 litres of alcohol and beer in total, and 200 cigarettes, 50 cigars or 250 g of tobacco, for adults 18 and over, whether you arrive by air, land or on foot. Declare cash above US$10,000; above US$100,000 you must also show where the money came from. Plant products are allowed up to 5 kg without a certificate.
Medicines with narcotic or psychotropic substances are allowed on medical grounds with documents naming the medicine and quantity, in Russian or with a notarised Russian translation.

saudi-arabia.h: What stands out when you travel to Saudi Arabia
p: Saudi Arabia bans importing alcohol and intoxicants of all kinds, with confiscation, fines and imprisonment. ZATCA exempts up to 200 cigarettes; 200 to 2,400 are allowed with duties and Saudi Food and Drug Authority approval. Declare cash above SAR 60,000, and goods in commercial quantities worth more than SAR 3,000.

The UK government says agricultural seeds may need special approval. Controlled drugs containing narcotic or psychotropic substances need a clearance permit from the SFDA, applied for online with a prescription and medical report.

serbia.h: What stands out when you travel to Serbia
p: Serbia's allowances are small: 1 litre of spirits or sparkling wine plus 1 litre of other wine, and 50 cigarettes, 25 cigarillos, 10 cigars or 50 g of tobacco. Declare €10,000 or more. Without inspection you may bring up to 5 kg of fresh fruit and vegetables, 100 g of seeds and up to three house plants, but only from European countries.
Customs says medicines containing controlled psychoactive substances need approval from the competent ministry before personal import.

seychelles.h: What stands out when you travel to Seychelles
p: Seychelles allows 2 litres of drinks up to 16% plus 2 litres of stronger drinks, and 250 g of tobacco or 200 cigarettes, for travellers 18 and over. Cash above SCR 50,000 goes through the red channel with a Cash Declaration Form and proof of where the money comes from. Live plants, vegetables and fresh fruit need written approval from the Department of Agriculture first.
Seychelles' filing to the UN narcotics board allows 30 days of narcotic drugs but 90 days of psychotropic substances, with a doctor's certificate endorsed in your home country.

singapore.h: What stands out when you travel to Singapore
p: Singapore gives duty-free liquor only after 48 hours abroad, not when arriving from Malaysia, and gives no duty-free concession on tobacco at all. Its HSA says travellers with e-vaporisers are fined and the items seized, and convicted foreigners can be deported. Report over S$20,000 on Form NP 727 within 72 hours of travel.

Amphetamine, the ingredient in Adderall, appears on Appendix A of the HSA document guide of controlled substances that need approval, which must be applied for at least two weeks before arrival, in English.

slovakia.h: What stands out when you travel to Slovakia
p: Slovakia follows the EU limits: 200 cigarettes by air but 40 by land or sea, the usual alcohol limits and a €10,000 cash declaration. Plants and seeds need a permit.

Its 2007 filing with the INCB allows 7 days for Schedule II psychotropic substances and 30 days for Schedules III and IV of the 1971 Convention, with a valid prescription, and says the Schengen agreement applies.

The Slovak Financial Administration allows 200 cigarettes plus ten packs of smokeless tobacco by air, but 40 cigarettes plus two packs by other transport, from age 17. Alcohol includes 2 litres of sparkling wine alongside 4 litres of still wine and 16 litres of beer. Cash of EUR 10,000 or more must be reported in writing to the border customs office, on form 1a for accompanied cash. Plants may be carried in small amounts only for use during the journey and without pest risk.

slovenia.h: What stands out when you travel to Slovenia
p: Slovenia applies the EU limits for arrivals from outside the EU (4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer, 200 cigarettes) and the €10,000 cash declaration. Plants and seeds need a permit.

Slovenia's Financial Administration says illicit drugs used as medicines may be carried within the Schengen area with a medical certificate issued or endorsed by the authority of your country of permanent residence.

Slovenia's tax administration (FURS) grants the tobacco and alcohol relief only for goods carried occasionally for personal or family use or as presents, never to under-17s. Cash of EUR 10,000 or more is declared on the official form at the EU external border. The food safety administration counts fruit, vegetables, potted plants, substrates, sowing material and cut flowers as plants, and most need a certificate and inspection on prior notification.

south-africa.h: What stands out when you travel to South Africa
p: South Africa allows 2 litres of wine plus 1 litre of spirits, and 200 cigarettes, 20 cigars and 250 g of tobacco, but under-18s cannot claim either allowance. South African banknotes above R100,000 can be seized without National Treasury permission, and you declare currency on the Traveller Declaration. Plants need a plant health import permit and soil is prohibited.
SAHPRA's guideline lets you hold a Schedule 3, 4, 5 or 6 medicine for personal use, up to one month's supply, with a valid prescription and a prescriber's certificate.

south-korea.h: What stands out when you travel to South Korea
p: South Korea allows 2 litres of liquor and 200 cigarette sticks, apart from the general US$800 allowance, and also 20 ml of e-cigarette liquid under 1% nicotine. Minors under 19 get no exemption. Report means of payment above US$10,000.
The MFDS requires handling approval for anyone, Korean or foreign, entering with narcotic or psychotropic drugs for their own treatment, a rule that has applied since 23 October 2009.

spain.h: What stands out when you travel to Spain
p: Spain follows the EU limits for arrivals from outside the EU (4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer, 200 cigarettes) and the €10,000 cash declaration. Plants and seeds need a permit.

Spain's AEMPS requires travellers entering with narcotic or psychotropic medicines to request a permit from its Narcotics and Psychotropics Area, authorising them to carry the medicine for their own treatment.

Spain's tax agency cuts tobacco to 80 cigarettes for residents and workers within 15 km of the Gibraltar border, and cuts allowances to one tenth for international transport staff. Cash of EUR 10,000 or more per person and trip is declared on form E1 or E2 for non-EU trips; movements within Spain are declared from EUR 100,000. Live plants must be declared whatever the quantity and must be free of soil, and potatoes and tubers must always be declared.

sri-lanka.h: What stands out when you travel to Sri Lanka
p: Sri Lanka Customs does not allow cigarettes, cigars, beedies or snuff in personal baggage at all, and WHO lists a ban on importing e-cigarettes. Tourists may bring 2 bottles of wine and 1.5 litres of spirits, bought at a Sri Lanka duty-free shop or brought from abroad on the day of arrival. Declare more than US$15,000 coming in, and more than US$10,000 going out.
Any plant item needs a permit and must be shown to the Plant Quarantine Officer. The NMRA does not allow Schedule III medicines; ordinary personal medicine may be carried for your stay or 90 days.

sweden.h: What stands out when you travel to Sweden
p: Sweden applies the EU limits for arrivals from outside the EU (4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer, 200 cigarettes) and the €10,000 cash declaration. Tullverket allows 20 ml of nicotine e-liquid from another EU country, and from outside the EU SEK 5,000 by air or ferry, or SEK 3,500 in total.
Swedish Customs says narcotic or doping medicines may be brought only for medical purposes and personal use, proved with a prescription, pharmacy label or doctor's certificate.

switzerland.h: What stands out when you travel to Switzerland
p: Switzerland's duty-free allowance is per person per day: 5 litres of drinks up to 18% plus 1 litre above, and 250 cigarettes or 250 g of tobacco, from age 17. Customs allows 250 ml of nicotine liquid or 25 disposable vapes a day. No declaration is needed for cash, but from CHF 10,000 customs can ask where it comes from, and the amount is registered.
Swissmedic allows medicines containing narcotics up to a 30-day supply, ideally in hand luggage and original packaging, with a certificate for each medicine.

taiwan.h: What stands out when you travel to Taiwan
p: Taiwan allows 1.5 litres of alcohol (1 litre if it comes from Mainland China) and, from age 20, 200 cigarettes, 25 cigars or 1 pound of tobacco. E-cigarettes, e-liquid, snuff, snus, chewing tobacco and shisha tobacco are prohibited and can bring criminal penalties. Each passenger may not carry more than NT$100,000 and RMB 20,000, and no fresh fruit from any country is allowed.
For controlled drugs Taiwan allows up to a 6-month supply with a prescription, and clearance needs a statement certified by the TFDA.

thailand.h: What stands out when you travel to Thailand
p: Thailand allows 1 litre of alcohol and 200 cigarettes or 250 g of tobacco; excess must be dropped in the box provided by Customs, or you face prosecution. The government says importing e-cigarettes can mean up to 10 years in prison or a fine of 5 times the product price. Declare foreign currency over US$15,000, although Customs' English page still shows an older US$20,000 threshold.
The FDA sorts travellers' controlled medicines by schedule, and for a psychotropic a supply of up to 30 days needs only a certificate or prescription.

turkey.h: What stands out when you travel to Turkey
p: Turkey allows 1 litre of drinks over 22% plus 2 litres up to 22%, and the high figure of 600 cigarettes, 50 cigars and 250 g each of cut and pipe tobacco. Cash above €10,000 or TL 25,000 must be declared, and an undeclared amount means a 10% fine, all the cash held and a report to the prosecutor. WHO lists an import ban on e-cigarettes with a personal-use exception.

Seeds, seedlings and cuttings are banned in luggage; up to 3 kg of fruit and vegetables and one bouquet are allowed. Medication for personal treatment is allowed with a document, sent up to a month before or three months after arrival.

ukraine.h: What stands out when you travel to Ukraine
p: Ukraine allows adults 5 litres of beer, 2 litres of wine and 1 litre of strong drinks, and 200 cigarettes, 50 cigars or 250 g of tobacco, without a written declaration. Absence of under 24 hours means no duty-free alcohol or tobacco. A written declaration is needed from €10,000.
Plant material in baggage is inspected under the plant quarantine law. Ukraine's filing to the UN narcotics board needs a valid prescription, a customs declaration and your passport.

united-arab-emirates.h: What stands out when you travel to the United Arab Emirates
p: Dubai's Passenger Customs Guide allows up to 4 litres of alcohol or 2 cartons of beer, with alcohol treated as a restricted item. Tobacco is 200 cigarettes, 50 cigars or 500 g. Dubai Customs lists e-cigarettes as restricted goods released only with approval. Declare cash over AED 60,000.

Plants and seedlings need a permit, and seedlings containing soil are not allowed. Adderall's amphetamine is on the UAE list as Psychotropic Schedule II, and pseudoephedrine is listed as controlled under the 1988 UN Convention.

united-kingdom.h: What stands out when you travel to the United Kingdom
p: Great Britain's allowance is 42 litres of beer, 18 litres of still wine and 4 litres of spirits, the largest alcohol allowance among these hubs, for travellers 17 and over. Tobacco is 200 cigarettes or 250 g, and you may bring up to 50 ml of vaping liquid. Declare £10,000 or more to Border Force. Other goods are worth up to £390.

The Home Office's personal-licence guidance works on a three-month rule: amphetamine is a Schedule 2 drug, and a supply of up to three months dispensed to you in your country of residence needs no licence.

united-states.h: What stands out when you travel to the United States
p: The US returning-resident exemption is 1 litre of alcohol, for adults 21 and over, and 200 cigarettes and 100 cigars, with a separate $800 goods exemption every 31 days after at least 48 hours abroad. Report currency over $10,000 on FinCEN Form 105; families and groups are counted together.
For medicines, the DEA generally decides whether a controlled substance may be imported for personal use, and the FDA coordinates with it on products under both agencies.

vietnam.h: What stands out when you travel to Vietnam
p: Vietnam's duty-free allowance is per entry: 1.5 litres of alcohol above 20%, 2 litres below 20%, or 3 litres of alcoholic drinks and beer, and 200 cigarettes, 20 cigars or 250 g of raw tobacco, with no allowance under 18. WHO lists a ban on importing e-cigarettes. Declare cash above US$5,000 or VND 15,000,000.

Plant items in hand or checked luggage must be declared and inspected before customs clearance. Vietnam Customs allows medicines for your own treatment of up to 7 days' use for narcotic drugs or up to 10 days' use for psychotropic and precursor drugs, citing Decree 54/2017.

kenya.h: What the Kenya Revenue Authority says about plants
p: The Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) passenger terminal clearance guide has a list of restricted items, and "Plants and Plant material" is on it. The guide says the list includes, but is not limited to, the items it names, so a plant product that is not spelled out can still be treated as restricted.

For restricted goods the guide says authorization from the relevant government institution is needed, through the licence or permit that applies, and the importer must present that permit or licence to the Customs officer before the goods are processed and released. The guide does not name the agency that issues a plant permit, and it does not list plants as prohibited. We could not open a Kenyan plant-health page that covers travellers, so ask the Kenyan authority for the permit rules before you bring any plant, seed or cutting.
kenya.src: Source read: KRA, passenger terminal clearance in Kenya (restricted items). It does not name the plant-health agency or give a traveller allowance.

georgia.h: What the Revenue Service of Georgia says about plants
p: In its customs brochure on exemptions and declaring, the Revenue Service of Georgia lists the goods that need a permit or certificate in addition to the normal customs steps. The list includes plants and animals, their parts or derivatives, next to weapons, narcotics, medicines and antiques.

The brochure also says an individual must declare goods when their import is restricted or needs a permit or licence. For a traveller that means a plant, seed or cutting should be declared and the permit or certificate shown, instead of being carried through unannounced. The brochure does not say which office issues a plant permit or what it requires, so we cannot give you those steps.
georgia.src: Source read: Revenue Service of Georgia, brochure on exemption of goods from duties and declaring. It does not name the issuing office.

morocco.h: What Moroccan Customs requires for plant products
p: Moroccan Customs states that admitting plant products requires a phytosanitary certificate issued by the competent services of ONSSA, the national food safety office. A phytosanitary certificate is the plant-health document that the exporting country's authority issues for a plant consignment, so for a traveller it is something to obtain before the trip, not at the airport.

The Customs traveller guide that we link also covers alcohol, tobacco and gifts. Today we could not open that PDF, so this page repeats the plant rule exactly as it is stated on our card and adds nothing beyond it. We have no source that gives a quantity allowance, a list of banned plants or an ONSSA contact for travellers.
morocco.src: Source: Moroccan Customs traveller guide as quoted on our card. The PDF could not be opened on the day this text was written.

jordan.h: Plants and seeds in Jordan: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: We have no card figure for Jordan because we found no readable official page for it.

The official page could not be re-opened, and the UK government's travel advice for Jordan, which we also read, says nothing about plants. So this section applies the general rule most countries follow: most countries ask for a plant health certificate from the country of origin for plants and seeds, ban soil, and seize or destroy plants that arrive without papers. We have no figure for Jordan, so ask Jordan Customs before you travel.
jordan.src: Official page not re-opened; the UK government (FCDO) advice read on 16 November 2026 does not cover plants. Global rule applied, unofficial.

argentina.h: What SENASA says about plants, seeds and fresh produce
p: Argentina's agriculture health service SENASA lists, under products travellers may not bring in, fresh fruit and vegetables, flowers and garden plants, fruit, ornamental and forest plants, and plant parts such as seeds, roots and buds. Only processed plant foods are listed as allowed, for example canned vegetables, fruit in syrup or vinegar, dried, roasted or salted products such as peanuts and almonds, potato chips, jams, candied fruit and juices.

The page says SENASA staff may confiscate products that lack the required authorisations and points to Resolución 295/1999 for the full rules. It does not mention a declaration for these items and gives no fines. Because the list names seeds and garden plants as not permitted, the practical advice is to leave them at home.
argentina.src: Source read: SENASA, Información al viajero (ingresar o regresar al país). No fines are stated on the page.

austria.h: What the Austrian government says about plants and seeds from outside the EU
p: The Austrian government portal says the rules apply to plants, plant products, seeds, soil and compost brought from non-EU countries, which may need a plant health certificate. Plants for planting and seeds may have to be inspected by the plant protection service at the border, and entry is possible only through customs offices that have such a service. Species protection rules apply as well, for example to live orchids.

Bananas, coconuts, dates, pineapples and durian from any non-EU country need no certificate. Plants, plant parts, fruit, vegetables, flowers and seeds from Switzerland, Liechtenstein and Northern Ireland need none either. The Canary Islands, Ceuta and Melilla and the French overseas territories count as non-EU for plant health. Questions go to the Federal Office for Food Safety plant protection service in Vienna, pflanzenschutzdienst@baes.gv.at. The page does not describe the inspection steps, airports or postal imports, and gives no fines.

The Austrian Federal Ministry of Finance customs page fills the gaps. Goods that need a certificate must be declared on arrival at customs, with the certificate: at Vienna, Linz, Salzburg, Innsbruck, Graz and Klagenfurt airports that means the red channel, never the green one, and failing to declare can have tax and criminal consequences. Goods that also need official controls can enter only at the airports that offer them, Vienna, Graz and Linz. Plants for planting, seeds included, from non-EU countries other than Switzerland, Liechtenstein and Northern Ireland always need a certificate. Some invasive alien plants and their seeds, rooted cuttings and young plants are banned from the EU altogether.
austria.src: Source read: oesterreich.gv.at, Pflanzen, Saatgut, Erde etc. (in German). No fines or inspection steps are on the page. Also read 23 November 2026: Austrian Federal Ministry of Finance (bmf.gv.at), "Plants, plant parts, fruit, vegetables, flowers and seed" (English).

belgium.h: What the Belgian foreign ministry says about plants from outside the EU
p: A Belgian foreign ministry page on plant health says it is forbidden to bring plants into the EU from non-EU countries unless they come with an approved phytosanitary certificate. It names fruit, vegetables, seeds and cut flowers among the items covered, and lists pineapple, dates, bananas, coconut and durian as exceptions. It tells travellers not to bring home plants from a long journey, and warns that small parcels ordered online often escape thorough plant health checks, so buyers should ask for a certificate.

The page sets no Belgium-specific rules beyond the EU framework and mentions no penalties. The Belgian food safety agency AFSCA issues phytosanitary certificates for plants exported from Belgium, so a traveller arriving in Belgium needs a certificate from the plant authority of the country they come from. Ask AFSCA before you bring any plant, seed or cutting.

The Belgian food safety agency FASFC is stricter than a certificate for some items: travellers from outside the EU may not bring plants for planting at all in their luggage, meaning seeds, bulbs, tubers, cuttings, grafts and rooted plants. If found they are confiscated and destroyed. Fruit, vegetables, flowers and other plant products need a phytosanitary certificate from the country of origin, otherwise they are confiscated and destroyed on arrival; the certificate can be asked for through that country's IPPC contact point. The only fruit allowed without one are pineapples, coconuts, durian, bananas and dates.
belgium.src: Source read: Belgian Federal Public Service Foreign Affairs, Healthy plants concern all of us. It mentions no penalties. Also read 23 November 2026: FASFC (Federal Agency for the Safety of the Food Chain), "Plants and plant products" (fasfc.be, English).

brazil.h: What the Brazilian agriculture ministry says about plant parts
p: Brazil's agriculture ministry (MAPA) says fresh or dried plant parts such as leaves, branches, stems, trunks, pollen and flowers may enter in a traveller's baggage only if three conditions are met. They must come with a phytosanitary certificate issued by the federal agricultural authority of the country of origin and meeting Brazil's plant health import requirements, they must meet the entry conditions set by Brazil's plant health authority, and they must show no signs of pests.

You must declare these items in the customs declaration, the e-DBV of the Federal Revenue, and present them to the agricultural inspection service VIGIAGRO through the Bens a Declarar channel. If the conditions are not met, inspectors may seize and destroy the products, or return them to the country of origin, which the page allows only for road travel. It gives no fines and links to the full list of permitted and prohibited agricultural goods, updated February 2026. We read the first part of this long page only.
brazil.src: Source read: MAPA (gov.br), Partes de plantas frescas ou secas (in Portuguese), first 100,000 characters. No fines are stated.

australia.h: Plants and seeds in Australia: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says most seeds need a phytosanitary certificate and must meet the conditions in BICON, the import conditions system of the Department of Agriculture, and that seeds that do not meet them are not permitted entry. It comes from the seeds for sowing page that we link below the card.

We could not re-open the official page, so we checked the UK government's travel advice for Australia, an unofficial source. On food and plants it says that food, animal products and plant material count as quarantine risks and must be declared on the Incoming Passenger Card or put in the bins, with a heavy fine for breaking quarantine. Travellers most often lose plants and seeds at the border because they were not declared, so declaring is the safe step even when the item seems harmless. For Australia, the Australian Border Force decides what may stay.
australia.src: UK government (FCDO) entry requirements page, read 16 November 2026. It is an unofficial source: it is another country's travel advice.

bahrain.h: What the Travel Doc customs page says about plants and seeds in Bahrain
p: The Travel Doc customs page for Bahrain says fruit, vegetables, plants and their derivative products need a permit from the Ministry of Municipalities and Agriculture Affairs. Palm tree seedlings need a permit to leave the country. It does not mention seeds separately.
The page names no publisher and shows no date, so confirm the figures with the customs authority before you travel.
bahrain.src: Unofficial source, read 16 November 2026: Travel Doc customs information page for Bahrain (infopages.traveldoc.aero, undated; it names no publisher). The official customs site could not be read.

cambodia.h: What the Cambodian plant quarantine Prakas says
p: Prakas No. 346 of Cambodia's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries sets the procedures for plant quarantine inspection of imports, exports and transit. It applies to people and companies that import any plant quarantine material, and it asks them to apply for inspection at the Plant Quarantine Inspection Office with a phytosanitary certificate from the exporting country, a fumigation certificate if the goods were fumigated, and an import licence for agricultural materials such as crops, fertilisers and chemicals.

For goods the Prakas classes as high risk, the importer must first get an Import Certificate or Permit for Plant Quarantine Materials from the General Directorate of Agriculture, which answers the risk analysis within 15 days. The Prakas is written for consignments and does not set an allowance for a tourist's personal plants or seeds, so the card's advice to ask before bringing any plant material stands. We read a copy of the Prakas held in the FAO legal database, not a page of the ministry.
cambodia.src: Source read: Prakas No. 346 PrK.KSK on plant quarantine inspection (MAFF), as published in the FAO FAOLEX database. It sets no traveller allowance.

canada.h: What the Canadian Food Inspection Agency says about plants and seeds
p: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency says plants, seeds and other plant material must not be a regulated pest or an invasive species before you pack them for return to Canada, because those items can spread in farm and natural areas and cause economic and environmental damage. Some seeds bought abroad may count as invasive species in Canada, and the agency has a seed identification page for that.

At the border you must declare all food, plant products including seeds, and any farm visits abroad. The page does not mention permits, soil or penalties for plants and seeds, and for animals it only says that missing paperwork can cause delays or refusal of entry. Check the agency's directive on regulated pests before you pack a plant or seed.
canada.src: Source read: CFIA, Travellers guide: tips for avoiding problems. Permits, soil and penalties are not on the page.

chile.h: What the Chilean agriculture service (SAG) says about the sworn declaration
p: Chile's agriculture and livestock service SAG requires a sworn declaration saying whether you carry plant or animal products, parts or by-products, or agricultural-use items in your clothing or luggage, whatever the quantity and however long ago you got them. The plant products it names are fruit and vegetables, seeds and grains, live plants and plant parts, flowers, soil, wood, cones, biological material, pesticides and fertilisers. An SAG inspector then checks whether what you carry meets Chile's entry rules, whether you declared it or not, by hand, by X-ray or with the SAG dog brigade.

You can file the form online up to one day before arrival, and you need a new form for every entry because it is valid only for the arrival date you enter. Paper forms are available at border crossings. People over 18 must file, parents or guardians declare for minors, and giving false information can lead to a fine and other measures by the health authority. The page does not name the amount of the fine.
chile.src: Source read: SAG, Declaración jurada SAG sobre ingreso de productos de origen vegetal o animal a Chile (in Spanish). The fine amount is not on the page.

china.h: What the Travel Doc customs page says about plants and seeds in China
p: The Travel Doc customs page for China says plants and their derivative products must be declared and are subject to restrictions and quarantine on arrival. Exporting endangered and rare plants, their seeds and reproducing materials is prohibited.
The page names no publisher and shows no date, so confirm the figures with the customs authority before you travel.
china.src: Unofficial source, read 16 November 2026: Travel Doc customs information page for China (infopages.traveldoc.aero, undated; it names no publisher). The official customs site could not be read.

colombia.h: Plants and seeds in Colombia: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says plant products in a traveller's baggage must come with the phytosanitary certificate of the country they come from, that non-compliant plants, planting material and fresh produce can be seized and incinerated, and that plants must be declared on the baggage declaration. It comes from a 2017 notice of the Colombian agriculture institute ICA.

The official page could not be re-opened, and the UK government's travel advice for Colombia, which we also read, says nothing about plants. So this section applies the general rule most countries follow: plant imports are among the most tightly controlled goods: certificate, inspection, and destruction of non-compliant material are the common rules. Ask the customs authority DIAN what applies in Colombia before you pack seeds or cuttings.
colombia.src: Official page not re-opened; the UK government (FCDO) advice read on 16 November 2026 does not cover plants. Global rule applied, unofficial.

bulgaria.h: Plants and seeds in Bulgaria: the card, the Bulgarian phytosanitary ordinance and an unofficial source
p: Bulgaria's Ordinance No. 8 of 27 February 2015 on phytosanitary control (as amended in 2018, published by the Ministry of Agriculture) names the Bulgarian Food Safety Agency as the only competent state body for plant-health control, and says imports of regulated plants and plant products go through border inspection points at the border crossings. Article 19 says no control and no certificate are needed where there is no pest risk and the plants are not on its restricted list, have no special requirements, and are brought in small quantities for the traveller's own consumption during the journey. Inspectors can release a consignment, hold it for a laboratory test, or place it under quarantine.

Our card gives the EU rule that applies in Bulgaria: plants and seeds from outside the EU generally need a phytosanitary certificate from the country they come from, and soil should not be packed. The Bulgarian customs agency and the Bulgarian Food Safety Agency (BFSA) apply this at the border.

We could not re-open the official page, so we checked the UK government's travel advice for Bulgaria, an unofficial source. On food and plants it says that meat, milk and products containing them cannot be taken into EU countries, with exceptions such as baby milk, baby food and special medical foods. It says nothing about live plants or seeds, so the general rule applies there: even a single packet of seeds can need a certificate, because the point of the rule is to keep pests and weeds out, not to count quantities. the Bulgarian National Customs Agency applies this in Bulgaria.

The ordinance is older than the current EU plant-health regulation, which is stricter for seeds and plants brought from outside the EU. We therefore keep the EU rule above as the safe one: do not count on the small-quantity exception for seeds or plants for planting, and ask the Bulgarian Food Safety Agency before you bring them.
bulgaria.src: Source read: Ordinance No. 8 of 27 February 2015 on phytosanitary control (mzh.government.bg, in Bulgarian), read 24 November 2026; it may have been overtaken by EU rules. The UK government (FCDO) entry requirements page, read 16 November 2026, is an unofficial source: it is another country's travel advice.

croatia.h: What Croatian Customs says about plants in luggage
p: The Croatian Customs Administration says some plants and plant products can come in a traveller's luggage only with a phytosanitary certificate from the competent authority of the exporting country. The permitted list is in Annexes XI and XII of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2072. Prohibited items are banned in any quantity and confiscated, and restricted items are allowed only in quantities for the personal use of the traveller or family. Pineapple, coconut, durian, bananas and dates need no certificate.

Seeds and plants for planting need a certificate and must be inspected by State Inspectorate inspectors at a border inspection post. The page names the posts: Bajakovo, Karasovići, Nova Sela, Ploče port, Rijeka port, Stara Gradiška and Zagreb airport. Failing to declare these items to customs is an offence punishable by a fine, and non-compliant items are confiscated for destruction. The page gives no fine amounts and no weight limits. Questions go to the State Inspectorate phytosanitary sector in Zagreb.

The Croatian page adds that the lists of plants allowed in with a third-country certificate are set by Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2021/2285 (Annex XI, parts A and B, and Annex XII).
