It says seeds and planting material may not be brought in through any other Croatian border crossing than those inspection posts, and that seeds or plants on the banned-species list, or any that skip the mandatory inspection, are always taken from the traveller. The inspectors work in the State Inspectorate's agriculture and plant health inspection sector, whose address on the page is Šubićeva 29, Zagreb.
croatia.src: Source read: Carinska uprava, Imports of plants and plant products in passengers personal luggage (English). Fine amounts are not on the page.

cyprus.h: What Cyprus Customs, the Cyprus Tourism Organisation and the Department of Agriculture say
p: The Cyprus Customs and Excise list for passengers names flowers and plants as a restricted import. It needs three things: a licence from the Director of the Department of Agriculture, a phytosanitary certificate from the country of origin, and a phytosanitary inspection by the Department.

The Cyprus Tourism Organisation's entry-requirements page covers seeds too: fruit, vegetables, cut flowers, dry nuts, seeds, bulbs, cuttings and wood products may not be brought in without a licence from the Director of Agriculture. On arrival they must be declared at customs and are kept for inspection by agricultural officers. Breaking the law can mean a fine or imprisonment.

In July 2026 the Department of Agriculture, as reported by the Cyprus Mail, told travellers to avoid bringing plants, seeds or plant products at all, even one souvenir plant or packet of seeds, because of pests such as the red palm weevil, and to ask for guidance first.
cyprus.src: Official sources: Cyprus Customs and Excise passenger restrictions list; Cyprus Tourism Organisation entry-requirements page (visitcyprus.com), both read 23 November 2026. The Department of Agriculture warning is taken from the Cyprus Mail report of 6 July 2026, an unofficial relay of an official statement.

czechia.h: What the Czech plant authority (ÚKZÚZ) says about importing plants
p: The Central Institute for Supervising and Testing in Agriculture (ÚKZÚZ) says no import permit is needed to bring plants from outside the EU, but plants with roots generally need a plant health certificate from the exporting country's plant protection service, and certain plants are banned under Annex 3 of Decree 215/2008. Commercial importers must register, but private use and consumption during transport are exempt. Animal and plant species protected by CITES need export and import permits.

The page also lists small non-commercial amounts that it says need no certificate and no inspection at entry: 2 kg of fruit and vegetables, one bouquet of cut flowers, and 5 original retail packets of seeds, not counting potato seed. That table comes from the national decree. Because EU plant health rules also apply and other Czech guidance says all seed needs a certificate, we cannot be sure the seed exception still holds, and we advise you not to rely on it. The page does not address travellers directly and gives no fines. Ask ÚKZÚZ before you bring seeds.
czechia.src: Source read: ÚKZÚZ, Fytosanitární požadavky při dovozu rostlin do ČR (in Czech). The small-quantity table may be out of date and the page gives no fines.

denmark.h: What Danish Customs says about plants in luggage
p: Danish Customs says private individuals can bring most common plants from other EU countries for personal use without documents: plants, bulbs, fruit, vegetables, table potatoes, seeds and cut flowers. It adds that the Danish Agricultural Agency advises bringing only plants that look completely healthy. Under the CITES rules, buying and selling endangered plants listed in Appendix A is prohibited within the EU, except for artificially propagated plants.

From non-EU countries you must always carry a phytosanitary certificate, issued in the country where the plant was bought, for live plants, bouquets and fruit. You must also declare plants for import control in advance, and the Danish Agricultural Agency checks them for a fee. Pineapple, coconut, banana, durian and dates can be carried freely. Postal consignments of plants need a certificate too, and suspected violations are withheld and sent to the agency. For luggage the page gives no specific rule on confiscation or fines, only that an item that is not permitted is withheld and you may be fined.
denmark.src: Source read: Toldstyrelsen, Do you know whether you are allowed to bring your item into Denmark? (English). Fine amounts are not on the page.

costa-rica.h: Plants and seeds in Costa Rica: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says the State Phytosanitary Service (SFE) lists seeds, fruit, plants, cuttings, tubers and some plant-fibre souvenirs as plant items with phytosanitary requirements, that the requirements depend on the product and the country it comes from, and that plant material that enters without the legal procedure can be held or destroyed.

The official page could not be re-opened, and the UK government's travel advice for Costa Rica, which we also read, says nothing about plants. So this section applies the general rule most countries follow: most countries ask for a plant health certificate from the country of origin for plants and seeds, ban soil, and seize or destroy plants that arrive without papers. We could not confirm more for Costa Rica, so ask the Dirección General de Aduanas before you bring any plant or seed.
costa-rica.src: Official page not re-opened; the UK government (FCDO) advice read on 16 November 2026 does not cover plants. Global rule applied, unofficial.

cuba.h: Plants and seeds in Cuba: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says Cuban Customs lists plants or parts of plants, fresh fruit and vegetables and seeds as absolutely prohibited, that soil or organic matter in any form is prohibited too, and that canned vegetables of recognised brands are the exception the page lists. It comes from the plant and animal health provisions page of the Cuban customs service.

We could not re-open the official page, so we checked the UK government's travel advice for Cuba, an unofficial source. On food and plants it says that you cannot bring in meat products, milk, fresh fruit, vegetables, seeds or organic matter, with some exceptions. The worldwide norm is that live plants, seeds and cuttings need a permit or a phytosanitary certificate, and untreated soil is not allowed. For Cuba, confirm the detail with the Cuban customs service (Aduana General).
cuba.src: UK government (FCDO) entry requirements page, read 16 November 2026. It is an unofficial source: it is another country's travel advice.

dominican-republic.h: What a Dominican newspaper reports about airport plant checks
p: Our card repeats a December 2020 article in the newspaper Diario Libre, in which the head of the plant health department of the Dominican Agriculture Ministry says inspectors check bags and suitcases at airports and ports for fruit and other products without registration that could bring in plant pests. When they find a problem, the product is seized and sent for incineration at airports and the border, and trucks carrying produce are sent back to their country of origin.

The article does not give a full list of what a traveller may not bring, and it is a newspaper, not a ministry page, which is why the card is marked unofficial. We did not find a readable ministry page with the traveller rules, so we cannot list permits or allowances. Ask the Ministry of Agriculture before you bring any plant, seed or fresh fruit.
dominican-republic.src: Source read: Diario Libre, 27 December 2020. This is an unofficial source and gives no list of prohibited items.

egypt.h: What the Cairo Airport guide says about seeds and seedlings
p: The customs regulations page of Cairo International Airport's passenger guide says it is prohibited to bring any seeds or agricultural seedlings into Egypt, to stop the spread of pests, and that the quarantine office deals with such cases. It names no specific quarantine office and gives no contact details.

The page mentions no other plants, no fruit, no permit route and no penalty. An airport guide is not the Egyptian agriculture ministry, which is why the card is marked unofficial. Check with Egyptian quarantine before you bring any plant material.
egypt.src: Source read: Cairo Airport, passenger guide, customs regulations. It is an airport page, not a ministry page, and covers seeds and seedlings only.

estonia.h: What Estonian Customs says about plants and seeds
p: Estonian Customs (EMTA) says that for arrivals from non-EU countries, pineapples, coconuts, bananas, dates and durians can be brought in, or mailed, in reasonable quantities, and so can dried berries, fruit and vegetables and dried seeds and nuts for human consumption. All other plants, seeds, fresh fruit, vegetables and berries need a phytosanitary certificate from the country of origin and must pass plant health control at a border checkpoint. The page notes that under the simplified procedure, passengers may not carry these products or send them by post.

From other EU countries, plants and plant products may be brought in or mailed in reasonable quantities, and the page recommends buying plants from professional garden shops to lower the risk of spreading pests. Apple trees, pear trees and cotoneasters need a plant passport. The page does not mention confiscation. For plant questions it names the Agriculture and Food Board, +372 605 1710.

The same EMTA page has a separate note on hemp seeds and mushroom spawn. Estonia's Act on Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances and Precursors prohibits growing cannabis to make narcotics and growing mushrooms that contain psilocin or psilocybin. Hemp varieties with no more than 0.3% THC grown for fibre may be cultivated, and their seeds are sold in large, labelled and certified packages, not by the piece.
estonia.src: Source read: EMTA, Prohibited and restricted goods (English). Confiscation and fines are not on the page.

ethiopia.h: What Ethiopia Plant Quarantine Regulation No. 4/1992 says
p: Council of Ministers Regulation No. 4/1992 says all imported plants and other articles that may carry plant pests are subject to plant quarantine, and that plants include plant products and seeds. Nobody may import a plant listed in Schedule I without an import permit issued by the Minister of Agriculture, and those plants must come with a phytosanitary certificate. Schedule I lists many crops and also names fresh fruit and vegetables. The importation of anything on Schedule II is prohibited, though the Minister may approve it for scientific study under strict quarantine.

An inspector may seize infected or infested plants and have them treated, re-exported or destroyed at the owner's expense, and breaking the rules is punished under the Plant Protection Decree No. 56 of 1971. The regulation dates from 1992 and the lists can be changed by the Minister, so it may have been amended since. It is a legal text from a database, not a traveller page, and it sets no personal allowance. Ask the Ministry of Agriculture before you bring any plant.
ethiopia.src: Source read: Plant Quarantine Regulation No. 4/1992 (Negarit Gazeta), as published in FAO FAOLEX. It may have been amended since 1992.

fiji.h: What the Biosecurity Authority of Fiji says about plants and seeds
p: The Biosecurity Authority of Fiji (BAF) says travellers must declare plants, plant products, and seed, propagation and planting material, as well as used gardening, farming and recreational equipment. You get a passenger arrival card on the way to Fiji, and you must complete and sign it before you enter, because it is a legal document.

A false, misleading or incorrect declaration can lead to fines, prison or both, and the page warns of heavy penalties for not declaring regulated items. It does not list the prohibited items or describe a traveller permit process, and it links only to a list of approved seed sources under import requirements. Questions go to info@baf.com.fj or the nearest Biosecurity Office.
fiji.src: Source read: Biosecurity Authority of Fiji, Plant and plant products. The fine amounts and the prohibited list are not on the page.

finland.h: What the Finnish Food Authority (Ruokavirasto) says about plants as luggage
p: The Finnish Food Authority says live plants, seeds for sowing, fresh cut flowers and most fresh fruit, vegetables and herbs generally cannot come from outside the EU in luggage, because they need a phytosanitary certificate that travellers usually cannot get while abroad. The certificate applies to live plants, propagation material such as seeds, cuttings, bulbs and tubers, cut flowers and fresh produce. Fresh pineapple, banana, durian, coconut and date need none, and processed, dried, frozen or preserved plant products for personal use are allowed, for example tea, coffee, dried or roasted nuts and seeds, spices, dried herbs, rice and flour. Online orders need a certificate too.

Within the EU, seedlings, seeds, potted plants, fresh produce and cut flowers can generally be brought for personal use. Host plants of fire blight, such as apple and pear trees, need a plant passport with the Erwinia amylovora marking, which most EU countries do not issue, and seed potatoes must be obtained in Finland. The page does not mention penalties. Questions go to kasvinterveys@ruokavirasto.fi.
finland.src: Source read: Ruokavirasto, Kasvit ja kasvituotteet (in Finnish). Penalties are not on the page.

france.h: What French Customs says about travelling with plants
p: French Customs says travellers bringing plants or plant products into the EU from non-EU countries, except Andorra, Monaco and Switzerland, must present a phytosanitary certificate from the first specimen. You get it before you leave from the authority responsible for plant protection and show it to customs if you are checked on arrival. The page mentions no small-quantity exemption. Bananas, durians, coconuts, pineapples and dates need no certificate and have no quantity limit.

Its table lists soil and other substrates, grapevine and citrus plants and potatoes for planting as prohibited. Plants for planting must also be presented at a border control post on arrival, where inspectors issue a common health entry document that you show to customs together with the certificate. The page does not mention seizure or fines and points to a separate procedure page for travellers returning with plants.

The same page lists other rules that apply on top of the certificate. Plants and products from protected species need a CITES import permit shown to customs. Some fruit and vegetables from certain non-EU countries (the page cites Regulation 669/2009, annex I) are checked at the border and need a common entry document, and dried fruit from certain countries weighing over 20 kg gets reinforced health checks. Plants banned as narcotics, and the plants Stephania tetrandra and Aristolochia fangchi (decree 98-397 of 20 May 1998), are prohibited. Durians from Vietnam need an official certificate and border presentation above 5 kg fresh or 2 kg other. From French overseas departments the certificate is needed from the first gram. For questions, customs gives the free number 0 800 94 40 40 (+33 1 72 40 78 50 from abroad).
france.src: Source read: douane.gouv.fr, Comment voyager avec des plantes et végétaux ? (in French) and the customs procedure page for travellers bringing plants, fruit and vegetables from outside the EU (in French), read 24 November 2026. Seizure and fines are not on the pages.

germany.h: What German Customs says about plants in personal luggage
p: German Customs says travellers bringing live plants, plant parts such as cut flowers, fruit or seeds into Germany for personal use need a phytosanitary certificate from the country of origin, issued by that country's competent plant health authority. Pineapples, coconuts, durians, bananas and dates need none.

The German-language customs page adds a list of plants you may not bring from outside the EU at all, apart from Switzerland and Liechtenstein: most conifers, some broadleaf trees (sweet chestnut, oak and poplar from North America), fruit trees and photinia, grapevines, citrus plants, loose soil and growing media, nightshade plants, potato tubers and many grass species. Plants infested with especially dangerous pests are banned too. The certificate is issued by the plant protection authority of the holiday country, and the page says the rules exist to keep dangerous diseases and pests out of German and EU crops.

If you cannot show a certificate, or an explicit import ban applies, the goods are usually destroyed and you may have to pay for the destruction. You can also be expected to pay a fine for an unauthorised import. Responsibility lies mainly with the authorities of the federal states, and Customs only supports them through checks at borders and airports. For questions, the page says to contact the authority for your place of residence first, and it names the Federal Ministry of Food and Agriculture and the Julius Kühn Institute as sources of further information.
germany.src: Source read: zoll.de, Plant protection (English) and Pflanzen und Pflanzenprodukte im Reiseverkehr (in German, read 24 November 2026). Fine amounts are not on the pages.

hong-kong.h: What the Hong Kong plant import page says
p: The Hong Kong Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) page on plant imports says any imported plant must come with a licence issued by the Department under Section 4 of Cap. 207, and most plants also need a valid phytosanitary certificate from the competent authority of the country of origin. Some listed plants, such as rubber, cocoa and tea, also need fumigation or disinfection and post-entry quarantine, and others, such as citrus, banana and rice, must meet set conditions.

Seeds need a valid phytosanitary certificate but no import licence. Cut flowers need neither. Fruit and vegetables for eating are exempt from both, and so are grains, pulses and spices for eating or industrial use. Importing plant pests or soil needs the Director's authorisation, with soil from elsewhere in China outside Hong Kong exempt. Anyone who breaks the Ordinance without reasonable excuse commits an offence with a maximum fine of HK$10,000 and six months in prison. The page does not address travellers directly.
hong-kong.src: Source read: AFCD (Hong Kong), Plant import quarantine requirements. It does not address travellers directly.

hungary.h: What the Hungarian tax and customs authority says about plants in luggage
p: A passenger information article of the Hungarian tax and customs authority (NAV) says plants and plant products brought from outside the EU can enter only with a common entry document that the plant health border station of the county government office finalises. Pineapple, banana, date, durian and coconut have no quantity limit, and other plants for personal use are allowed up to 5 kg per person or one piece per person, for example 5 kg of apples or one melon.

The article says plants and plant products that cannot be eaten, such as seeds, living plants and wreaths, are not allowed, and that produce or plant parts with soil on them cannot be brought in. It does not name a phytosanitary certificate and does not describe baggage checks for plants. It is a news article and its date is not shown in the text we read, so check the current rules with NAV or the national food chain safety office before you travel.
hungary.src: Source read: NAV, Itt a vakáció! Mi lehet a poggyászban? (in Hungarian). The date and penalties are not shown in the text read.

greece.h: What the Greek authorities say about seeds arriving from outside the EU
p: The Region of Attica (Directorate of Agricultural Economy and Veterinary Medicine) relays a September 2020 notice from the Ministry of Rural Development and Food. It says that seeds entering the EU must come with a phytosanitary certificate and undergo a plant health check at the Union's points of entry, citing Regulation (EU) 2016/2031, Articles 72 and 73.

The notice was triggered by unrequested packets of seeds posted to private people from China, Singapore, Taiwan, Vanuatu and Malaysia, with no certificate and no label saying they were seeds. People who receive such seeds must not plant them or touch them with bare hands, and should hand the packets with their wrapping to the local plant health service. It is a rule for posted seeds, not a traveller allowance, and it gives no quantity limit for seeds in hand luggage.
greece.src: Source read on 22 November 2026: Region of Attica, "Ταχυδρομικά πακέτα μικροποσοτήτων σπόρων που αποστέλλονται σε ιδιώτες από τρίτες χώρες" (28 September 2020, in Greek). It covers posted seeds, not luggage.

iceland.h: What the Icelandic Food and Veterinary Authority says about plants
p: The Icelandic Food and Veterinary Authority (MAST) says importing plants needs a phytosanitary certificate and must meet regulation no. 189/1990. Travellers between countries may bring a few plants without a certificate, in the same quantities the page allows for parcel post: bouquets of cut flowers and branches up to 25 plants, bulbs, corms and tubers from Europe in unopened commercial packaging up to 2 kg, and up to 3 potted indoor plants from Europe. Someone moving house may bring up to 30 potted indoor plants from a European country, of the kind a typical household has.

Wild plants gathered outdoors, woody plants with or without roots, bonsai and potatoes are not covered by these exemptions, so they always need the certificate. The page does not mention penalties or a traveller permit. Check with MAST before you bring anything else, and note that the limits are for plants from Europe.
iceland.src: Source read: MAST, Import of plants (English). Penalties are not on the page.

india.h: What the Indian customs passenger guide says about plants
p: The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs guide for passengers lists plants and their produce, for example fruits and seeds, among restricted goods. It also lists live birds and animals, including pets, as restricted, and the list of prohibited goods includes wildlife products.

Restricted means the goods may enter only under conditions, but the guide does not say what those conditions are for plants, who issues a permit, what a traveller may carry or what the penalty is. We did not find a plant quarantine page for travellers. Check Indian customs and the plant quarantine authority before you bring any plant, seed or fruit.
india.src: Source read: CBIC, Customs clearance of passengers at a glance (PDF). It gives no conditions or penalties for plants.

italy.h: What the Italian Customs and Monopolies Agency says about plants
p: The Agenzia delle Dogane e dei Monopoli (ADM) traveller card of July 2025 says bringing in even small quantities of plants is not allowed without the phytosanitary certificates required from the country of origin, because of the danger of spreading harmful organisms. For plant foods or plant feed that need no certificate and are carried for personal use, it gives a general net weight limit of 5 kg for fresh products and 2 kg for dried products.

The card has a separate section for protected species, with CITES rules for plants such as cactus and orchids. We did not find a rule on seeds in luggage, and the card does not say what the penalty is for plants without a certificate. Check ADM or the regional plant health service before you bring any plant or seed to Italy.
italy.src: Source read: ADM, Carta doganale del viaggiatore (July 2025, in Italian). Seeds and penalties for plants are not covered in the part read.

indonesia.h: What the Travel Doc customs page says about plants and seeds in Indonesia
p: The Travel Doc customs page for Indonesia lists plants and their derivative products, such as vegetables and fruit, among restricted goods, which generally need a permit before arrival. It does not mention seeds.
The page names no publisher and shows no date, so confirm the figures with the customs authority before you travel.
indonesia.src: Unofficial source, read 16 November 2026: Travel Doc customs information page for Indonesia (infopages.traveldoc.aero, undated; it names no publisher). The official customs site could not be read.

ireland.h: What Irish Revenue and the Department of Agriculture say about plants brought in by passengers
p: The Revenue Tax and Duty Manual "Importation of plants and plant products" (last reviewed January 2026) names the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine (DAFM) as the authority that checks plants and plant products arriving from outside the EU. Revenue's Customs Service only refers consignments to DAFM.

Approved border control posts for plants are Dublin Port, Dublin Airport and Rosslare Europort. For passengers the manual says personal consignments of plants or plant products carried as luggage should be notified to DAFM plant health inspectors at the relevant post. It gives no allowance and no seed rule for travellers.

The Department of Agriculture's page on personal consignments (updated 12 June 2026) lists plants, fruit, vegetables, cut flowers, seeds, soil and timber as items that may not come in from a third country without a phytosanitary certificate shown at the point of entry. It counts Great Britain as a third country but not Northern Ireland, and exempts bananas, durians, dates, pineapples and coconuts.
ireland.src: Source read on 22 November 2026: Revenue, Tax and Duty Manual, Importation of plants and plant products (PDF, last reviewed January 2026). Also read on 23 November 2026: Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, "Information on Personal Consignments in Luggage or through Postal, Courier & Online Services".
link: Department of Agriculture: Personal consignments in luggage

israel.h: What the Travel Doc customs page says about plants and seeds in Israel
p: The Travel Doc customs page for Israel says plants and plant products are restricted and generally need a permit obtained before arrival. Exports are subject to Ministry of Agriculture inspection. It does not mention seeds specifically.
The page names no publisher and shows no date, so confirm the figures with the customs authority before you travel.
israel.src: Unofficial source, read 16 November 2026: Travel Doc customs information page for Israel (infopages.traveldoc.aero, undated; it names no publisher). The official customs site could not be read.

jamaica.h: What a Jamaican government news item says about plant permits
p: A Jamaica Information Service article of 16 September 2020 says travellers need a permit to bring plants and plant products into Jamaica, issued by the Plant Quarantine and Inspection Branch of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries, to protect farming from pests and diseases. You register as an importer on the Ministry's trade site, apply for a permit for the specific plant or plant product, pay online and receive the permit online, with no office visit. The branch's number given in the article is 876-977-6401.

The article does not state fees or penalties, and it does not cover the amnesty bins at the airports that our card mentions. It is a news article from 2020, so check the current steps with the Ministry before you travel.
jamaica.src: Source read: Jamaica Information Service, Permit required to import plants and plant products (16 September 2020). Fees, penalties and amnesty bins are not in it.

japan.h: What the Japanese Plant Protection Station says about carrying plants
p: Japan's plant protection service says travellers must present a phytosanitary certificate issued by the government of the exporting country, and that an import inspection is required by law whatever the quantity or purpose, even for small plants and duty-free purchases. You do it at the Plant Quarantine Counter after immigration and before customs. Plants that pass get a plant inspection passed stamp, and plants without it cannot clear customs. There is no inspection fee and most inspections are quick.

Soil and plants with soil attached are prohibited whatever their origin. The prohibited list also includes quarantine pests, rice straw and rice husks, with exceptions for the Korean Peninsula and Taiwan, and some fruit and vegetables depending on origin, listed in the importing conditions database. No import permit is required. Violations can lead to up to three years in prison or a fine of up to three million yen under the Plant Protection Act, and plants without the certificate may be disposed of. Some plants are exempt, so ask a Plant Protection Station.
japan.src: Source read: Plant Protection Station, MAFF Japan, introduction page (English).

latvia.h: What the Latvian Food and Veterinary Service says about plants for planting
p: The Latvian Food and Veterinary Service (PVD) page on goods in personal baggage says importing plants intended for planting, including seeds, needs a phytosanitary certificate from the competent authority of the third country, and that the plants must be presented to the Food and Veterinary Service for control. Up to 2 kg of fresh fruit, vegetables or nuts in shell is allowed with a third-country phytosanitary certificate, and above 2 kg of fresh fruit, vegetables and berries the products must be presented for control.

Processed non-animal foods such as bread, chocolate and pasta, and bananas, coconuts, dates, pineapples and durians, may be brought in without restriction. Products from Russia and Belarus are subject to separate bans that override these allowances. The page also sets food limits for personal baggage, for example 5 kg of listed fresh non-animal products, which is about food, not plants for planting. It does not describe penalties.

The Food and Veterinary Service's own infographic on what may enter Latvia from outside the EU lists what is prohibited for private individuals: plants of selected genera and species intended for planting, potatoes, soil and growing media (except clean peat and coconut fibre), and biological and chemical plant-protection products, and plants that are hosts of the Xylella fastidiosa bacterium from countries not declared free of it. With a phytosanitary certificate from the country of dispatch you may bring plants of other genera for planting, seeds for sowing and fresh unprocessed plant products, including shelled nuts. Bananas, durians, coconuts, dates and pineapples need no certificate.
latvia.src: Source read: Latvian Food and Veterinary Service, Food products (English). Penalties are not on the page. Also read 23 November 2026: Latvian Food and Veterinary Service (pvd.gov.lv), infographic on products allowed and prohibited from outside the EU (English PDF).

lebanon.h: What the Beirut airport website says about fresh fruit and vegetables
p: The Beirut airport website says fresh fruit and vegetables may carry fruit fly eggs and larvae too small to see, that limiting their entry protects Lebanese farmers from serious losses, and that travellers arriving in Lebanon are prohibited from carrying fresh fruit and vegetables.

The page does not mention plants or seeds, and it is an airport page, not the Lebanese agriculture ministry, which is why the card is marked unofficial. We did not find a readable ministry page on plants and seeds, so we cannot say what applies to them. Ask the Lebanese Ministry of Agriculture before you bring a plant or seed.
lebanon.src: Source read: Beirut airport (beirutairport.gov.lb) page on fresh fruit and vegetables. It does not cover plants or seeds.

kuwait.h: Plants and seeds in Kuwait: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says the GCC plant quarantine law, which Kuwait is part of, makes travellers' plants subject to inspection, makes not declaring them an offence, and excludes anything meant for planting from the certificate exemption. It comes from a document of the GCC secretariat, which is why the card is marked unofficial for Kuwait.

The official page could not be re-opened, and the UK government's travel advice for Kuwait, which we also read, says nothing about plants. So this section applies the general rule most countries follow: soil, fresh fruit and cuttings are the items most often refused, and plants that pass usually pass only with a certificate and an inspection. Kuwait Customs sets the details for Kuwait.
kuwait.src: Official page not re-opened; the UK government (FCDO) advice read on 16 November 2026 does not cover plants. Global rule applied, unofficial.

lithuania.h: Plants and seeds in Lithuania: what the State Plant Service said in a news report
p: We could not open the State Plant Service site (vatzum.lrv.lt) or Lithuanian customs, so this section comes from an unofficial source: the news site Alkas.lt, in an article of 6 March 2022 that reports the Ministry of Agriculture and the State Plant Service. It is a news report, not an official page, and it is from 2022.

The ministry proposed setting up border plant health posts at Vilnius airport and at the national post operator Lietuvos paštas, because even small amounts of seeds or planting material can carry harmful bacteria or viruses. The article says plants for planting and seeds from outside the EU must travel through plant health posts and carry a phytosanitary certificate from the exporting country. It quotes the head of the Service's border control coordination unit: every consignment of plants, plant products and other objects from a non-EU country needs a certificate and a plant health check before it is released to the customer. It gives no luggage allowance and no seed quantity.
lithuania.src: Unofficial source, read on 22 November 2026: Alkas.lt, "Siūloma stiprinti įvežamų augalų ir sėklų patikrą" (6 March 2022, in Lithuanian), quoting the State Plant Service. The official Lithuanian pages returned a Cloudflare block.

mexico.h: What SENASICA said about plants and seeds in a travellers press release
p: A press release of the Mexican agri-food health service SENASICA dated 19 December 2014 says propagative plant material, including seeds, bulbs and cuttings, as well as cut flowers, live plants, dry grains and cereals and fresh fruit and vegetables, is regulated and must meet SENASICA's published import requirements. Soil, straw, hay and palm are prohibited under any circumstances.

The release tells travellers to research the rules before the trip and to declare all the products they carry at ports, airports and border crossings, and it warns that the rules can change at any time. It mentions no penalties. It is more than ten years old and was written for the winter holiday season, so check the current requirement modules on the SENASICA site before you bring any plant or seed.
mexico.src: Source read: SENASICA, press release of 19 December 2014 (Spanish). It is old and gives no penalties.

nepal.h: What the Nepal aeronautical information publication says about plants
p: The aeronautical information publication of the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, in its customs section, lists the documents needed to clear regulated goods from the quarantine office before customs. Plants and plant products, biological control agents and means of growing plants such as soil, moss and peat need an entry permit issued beforehand by the Plant Quarantine and Pesticide Management Centre under the Plant Protection Act 2007, together with a phytosanitary certificate from the country of export.

It adds that protected plant species listed under CITES need prior permission from the authority concerned, along with a phytosanitary certificate for any plants or plant products regulated under the Plant Protection Act. The publication is written about consignments and is an aviation document, not a page of the plant quarantine centre, so it sets no personal allowance and no penalty. Ask the centre before you bring a plant.
nepal.src: Source read: Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, AIP Nepal (customs and quarantine section). It sets no traveller allowance or penalty.

malaysia.h: What the Travel Doc customs page says about plants and seeds in Malaysia
p: The Travel Doc customs page for Malaysia says plants and their derivative products are restricted and generally need a permit before arrival. Exporting plants, including orchids, also needs a permit. Seeds are not listed specifically, apart from palm kernels and seeds on the export side.
The page names no publisher and shows no date, so confirm the figures with the customs authority before you travel.
malaysia.src: Unofficial source, read 16 November 2026: Travel Doc customs information page for Malaysia (infopages.traveldoc.aero, undated; it names no publisher). The official customs site could not be read.

maldives.h: What the Travel Doc customs page says about plants and seeds in the Maldives
p: The Travel Doc customs page for the Maldives says live plants and their derivative products need a phytosanitary certificate and must be inspected and approved by the Ministry of Fisheries and Agriculture. It does not mention seeds.
The page names no publisher and shows no date, so confirm the figures with the customs authority before you travel.
maldives.src: Unofficial source, read 16 November 2026: Travel Doc customs information page for the Maldives (infopages.traveldoc.aero, undated; it names no publisher). The official customs site could not be read.
link: Travel Doc: the Maldives customs information

mauritius.h: What the Travel Doc customs page says about plants and seeds in Mauritius
p: The Travel Doc customs page for Mauritius says plants and their derivative products, such as fruit, vegetables and seeds, need clearance from the Ministry of Agro-Industry and Food Security. Sugarcane cuttings and plants are prohibited.
The page names no publisher and shows no date, so confirm the figures with the customs authority before you travel.
mauritius.src: Unofficial source, read 16 November 2026: Travel Doc customs information page for Mauritius (infopages.traveldoc.aero, undated; it names no publisher). The official customs site could not be read.

luxembourg.h: What Luxembourg's agriculture ministry says about plants from outside the EU
p: The Administration des services techniques de l'agriculture (ASTA), part of the Ministry of Agriculture, Viticulture and Rural Development, asks travellers not to bring any plant material into the EU from outside it. Its press release of 7 August 2023 names plants, seeds, roots, fruit and vegetables bought as souvenirs as ways for pests to reach gardens and fields.

It gives two examples. The oriental fruit fly (Bactrocera dorsalis) could damage plum and cherry orchards in Luxembourg, and invasions have already happened in Italy. The bacterium Xylella fastidiosa, spread by infected plants, killed millions of olive trees in Puglia. ASTA also says customs officers confiscate plants in personal luggage at EU entry points when no phytosanitary certificate from the country of origin comes with them, and it backs the EU campaign slogan: take photos, do not bring plants home. The release gives no quantity limit and says nothing about seeds separately.
luxembourg.src: Source read on 22 November 2026: gouvernement.lu, press release "La santé des plantes, c'est la santé pour tous" (ASTA, 7 August 2023, in French). Quantity limits, seeds and fines are not on the page.

malta.h: What Malta's Plant Protection Directorate does at the border
p: A Malta Public Service article of 1 February 2023 describes the Plant Protection Directorate as the body that protects plants, seeds and other propagation material from pests and diseases. Its Monitoring and Control Unit manages import controls and the internal market and inspects greenhouses, fields, nurseries and public gardens.

Its diagnostic laboratory tests plant samples for bacteria, viruses, moulds, nematodes and insects, including imported plants. The article does not set a traveller allowance, a seed rule or a penalty, so for a specific plant or seed, ask the Directorate before you travel.

The Directorate's own inspection page says plant material entering Malta is checked at Border Control Posts, and that consignments from third countries get identity, physical and document checks. Malta also joined the EU #PlantHealth4Life campaign through its Food Safety and Security Authority: in January 2026 it reminded travellers that plants, seeds, soil or cuttings, even as gifts or souvenirs, can carry pests, so the safe choice is to leave them where they are.
malta.src: Source read on 22 November 2026: Malta Public Service, "The work of the Plant Protection Directorate" (1 February 2023). It describes the Directorate, not a traveller allowance. Also read 23 November 2026: Plant Protection Directorate, "Inspectorate and enforcement" (Government of Malta), and Malta Daily, 6 January 2026, on the #PlantHealth4Life reminder (a news report, so a reliable but unofficial source).

netherlands.h: What the Dutch food safety authority (NVWA) says about bringing plants
p: The Dutch Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) says fresh vegetables, fruit or flowers from outside the EU need a phytosanitary certificate issued by the authority of the country you leave, and so do plants, seeds, nuts and bulbs. Fresh bananas, coconuts, dates, pineapples and durians need none, nor do processed fruit, dried flowers, seeds and nuts meant for eating if the packaging shows what they are, and dried plant material. Fresh produce, plants, seeds, nuts and bulbs from Switzerland, Liechtenstein and Northern Ireland are exempt, while travel from the rest of the UK and from the Canary Islands falls under the strict rules.

Plants, seeds, nuts and bulbs must be inspected by the NVWA on arrival: you report to customs at the red exit marked something to declare. If you travel by car, bus or train you are inspected at the first point of entry into the EU. Protected species such as cacti and orchids need a CITES permit and sometimes an EU certificate. The page does not describe what happens to goods without a certificate or any fine. The IPPC website lists the contacts that issue certificates in each country.
netherlands.src: Source read: NVWA, Ik wil planten of plantaardige producten meenemen naar Nederland (in Dutch). Destruction and fines are not on the page.

norway.h: What Norwegian Customs says about plants, seeds and flowers
p: Norwegian Customs lists the amounts a traveller may bring without a permit: up to 10 kg of fruit, berries and vegetables, 25 cut flowers, 3 kg of flower bulbs and tubers, 5 potted houseplants from European countries and 50 seed packets. Larger amounts need a phytosanitary certificate for the goods. Potatoes need a special permit whatever the quantity.

Bringing pesticides into Norway is prohibited, whether for professional use, unless approved by the competent authority, or for your own garden. The page does not treat EU and non-EU travellers differently and gives no penalties. For anything else it sends you to the Norwegian Food Safety Authority, Mattilsynet. Because Norway is not in the EU, these limits are Norway's own, not the EU rule.
norway.src: Source read: Toll.no, Regulations for fruits, vegetables, plants, flowers and seeds (English). Penalties are not on the page.

nigeria.h: What the UK government advice says about fruit and cereals in Nigeria
p: Our card repeats the UK government's travel advice for Nigeria, which we re-read today: it is illegal to import beer, mineral water, soft drinks, sparkling wine, fruits, vegetables and cereals into Nigeria. The advice says nothing about plants or seeds. It says only that strict rules apply to goods, that anything that may be prohibited or subject to duty must be declared, and it links to Nigeria's customs website for the full list.

This is the advice of another country's government, which is why the card is marked unofficial. We did not find a readable Nigerian agriculture or customs page on plants and seeds, so we cannot say what applies to them. Ask the Nigeria Agricultural Quarantine Service before you bring any plant or seed.
nigeria.src: Source read: UK government (FCDO), Nigeria entry requirements. It is an unofficial source and does not cover plants or seeds.

new-zealand.h: Plants and seeds in New Zealand: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says seeds, bulbs, flowers and soil are biosecurity risk goods, that you must declare them or put them in the disposal bins, and that failing to do so can bring a NZD 400 fine. It comes from the Ministry for Primary Industries page on how to declare items that we link below the card.

We could not re-open the official page, so we checked the UK government's travel advice for New Zealand, an unofficial source. On food and plants it says that most food products are illegal to import and that breaking the rules can bring a fine of up to NZ$100,000 or prison. It says nothing about live plants or seeds, so the general rule applies there: travellers most often lose plants and seeds at the border because they were not declared, so declaring is the safe step even when the item seems harmless. For New Zealand, New Zealand Customs and the Ministry for Primary Industries decides what may stay.
new-zealand.src: UK government (FCDO) entry requirements page, read 16 November 2026. It is an unofficial source: it is another country's travel advice.

oman.h: Plants and seeds in Oman: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says Oman requires a phytosanitary certificate for seeds and live plants, a permit for some plants, and bans untreated soil, with fines up to OMR 1,000. It comes from the general information section of the Oman civil aviation publication that we link below the card.

The official page could not be re-opened, and the UK government's travel advice for Oman, which we also read, says nothing about plants. So this section applies the general rule most countries follow: soil, fresh fruit and cuttings are the items most often refused, and plants that pass usually pass only with a certificate and an inspection. Oman Customs sets the details for Oman.
oman.src: Official page not re-opened; the UK government (FCDO) advice read on 16 November 2026 does not cover plants. Global rule applied, unofficial.

panama.h: Plants and seeds in Panama: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says Tocumen airport states that every live plant and plant product must come with the phytosanitary certificate of its country of origin, and that the customs form asks whether you carry fruit, meat or food. We tried to re-read that airport page today and it only shows a notice that the airport website has moved to a new address.

The official page could not be re-opened, and the UK government's travel advice for Panama, which we also read, says nothing about plants. So this section applies the general rule most countries follow: plant imports are among the most tightly controlled goods: certificate, inspection, and destruction of non-compliant material are the common rules. Ask the Panamanian customs authority what applies in Panama before you pack seeds or cuttings.
panama.src: Official page not re-opened; the UK government (FCDO) advice read on 16 November 2026 does not cover plants. Global rule applied, unofficial.

portugal.h: What the Portuguese plant health authority (DGAV) says to tourists
p: The Portuguese Directorate-General for Food and Veterinary (DGAV) page for tourists, passengers and travellers warns that plants bought in non-EU countries can bring exotic pests and diseases into Portugal. It says plants for planting, whether potted, with substrate, bare-root or as roots, rhizomes, bulbs, layers or cuttings, carry a high plant health risk, and that some species are prohibited from entering Portugal.

Other plants, even if not meant for planting, need a phytosanitary certificate from the plant health authority of the exporting country. Some plant products not meant for planting may be exempt from inspection at the border but still need the certificate. Pineapple, banana, coconut, durian and date fruits need none to enter the EU. The page does not mention seeds specifically, a customs declaration or penalties, so ask DGAV before you bring any plant or seed.

The Portuguese Tax and Customs Authority's traveller guide (February 2026) fills the gap on seeds: it lists plant products, including fruit, plants and seeds, among the goods whose import from non-EU countries is prohibited or restricted, next to protected species and food of animal origin. It does not give a quantity or a fine, so the DGAV certificate rule above is the one to follow.
portugal.src: Source read: DGAV, Importação e exportação de vegetais: turistas, passageiros e viajantes (in Portuguese). Seeds, declaration and penalties are not on the page. Also read 23 November 2026: Autoridade Tributária e Aduaneira, "Guia do viajante" (February 2026, in Portuguese).

russia.h: What a Russian plant health office says about plant products carried by individuals
p: A page of the Northwestern Interregional Office of the Russian plant and animal health service Rosselkhoznadzor, last updated 6 January 2023, says citizens arriving in Russia must show quarantine plant products in hand luggage or baggage to a phytosanitary inspector at the border crossing. Seeds, planting material and potatoes must have a phytosanitary certificate from the exporting country's plant protection organisation. That covers seeds, bulbs, seedlings, tubers, rhizomes, cuttings, live plants with soil, including potted plants, and seed and food potatoes.

Without a certificate, a person may bring up to 5 kg of other plant products in luggage, but this allowance does not cover seeds, planting material or potatoes. Products infested with quarantine organisms are prohibited, and non-compliant items may be returned, seized or destroyed. The page gives an administrative fine of 300 to 500 rubles for individuals under Article 10.2 of the Code of Administrative Offences, and lists temporary restrictions for travellers from Ukraine, Moldova, Azerbaijan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Georgia. The page is more than two years old, so check for newer rules.
russia.src: Source read: Rosselkhoznadzor Northwestern Interregional Office page for individuals (in Russian), updated 6 January 2023.

qatar.h: What the Qatar customs restricted goods list says about plants
p: The Qatar General Authority of Customs restricted goods list names the authority responsible for plant items. Bulbs, tubers, corms and rhizomes, live plants and seedlings, including grapevines, palm tree seedlings, ornamental shrubs and roses, and cut flowers and foliage all fall under the Ministry of Municipality and Environment, Department of Agriculture Affairs and Fisheries. Vegetable, flower, sugar beet and alfalfa seeds are under the same department, and some seeds, such as potato and onion seeds, are also under the Ministry of Public Health.

The page lists the responsible authority but does not state what approval is needed, what a traveller may carry or what the penalty is. We read the first 100,000 characters of a long page and did not find poppy or hemp seeds there, so we cannot confirm what our card says about them. Ask the Department of Agriculture Affairs before you bring any plant, bulb or seed.
qatar.src: Source read: Qatar General Authority of Customs, Restricted goods (first 100,000 characters). It names authorities, not conditions.

peru.h: What the Travel Doc customs page says about plants and seeds in Peru
p: The Travel Doc customs page for Peru gives no personal allowance for plants or seeds. It lists agricultural products and flora and fauna as restricted goods that in most cases need a permit before arrival, and refers you to SUNAT for details.
The page names no publisher and shows no date, so confirm the figures with the customs authority before you travel.
peru.src: Unofficial source, read 16 November 2026: Travel Doc customs information page for Peru (infopages.traveldoc.aero, undated; it names no publisher). The official customs site could not be read.

philippines.h: What the Travel Doc customs page says about plants and seeds in the Philippines
p: The Travel Doc customs page for the Philippines says plants and their derivative products, such as fruit, are restricted and must come with a phytosanitary certificate from the port of origin. It does not mention seeds specifically.
The page names no publisher and shows no date, so confirm the figures with the customs authority before you travel.
philippines.src: Unofficial source, read 16 November 2026: Travel Doc customs information page for the Philippines (infopages.traveldoc.aero, undated; it names no publisher). The official customs site could not be read.
link: Travel Doc: the Philippines customs information

poland.h: What the Polish plant inspectorate (PIORiN) says about private imports of plants
p: PIORiN splits plant goods carried by private people into two groups. Plants that are not for planting, such as fresh fruit other than the five exempt ones, fresh vegetables, cut flowers and leaves, need a phytosanitary certificate from the country of origin and may come in through any border crossing.

Plants for planting (potted plants, seeds for sowing, seedlings, cuttings, tubers, bulbs, rhizomes) follow commercial rules even for one traveller. They need the certificate and must enter through a post designated for phytosanitary border inspection. The person must open a TRACES NT account, notify the consignment at least 24 hours before arrival (4 hours by air), and pay an inspection fee set in Annex IV of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The inspector then decides whether the plants may enter. Dried, frozen or otherwise processed fruit, vegetables and plant parts need no phytosanitary check. Ceuta, Melilla, the Canary Islands, Guadeloupe, French Guiana, Martinique, Réunion, Saint-Barthélemy and Saint-Martin count as non-EU for plant rules, while Madeira, the Azores, Northern Ireland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein count as EU.
poland.src: Source read on 22 November 2026: PIORiN (gov.pl), Rules for importing goods of plant origin from third countries ... by private individuals for personal use. Soil and penalties are not on the page.

serbia.h: What Serbian Customs says about bringing plants
p: Serbian Customs lists small quantities you may bring without a plant health inspection: up to 5 kg of fresh fruit and vegetables, not counting potatoes, one bouquet or wreath of cut flowers, up to 100 g of seeds or five packets of flower and vegetable seeds in original packaging, up to 3 kg of ornamental bulbs and tubers, up to 3 houseplants, excluding bonsai, and up to 10 balcony plants or non-woody ornamental shrubs. The plants must come from European countries, be for non-industrial and non-commercial use or for eating during the trip, and pose no risk of spreading harmful organisms.

Larger quantities need inspection, and you must report to a border crossing that has plant health inspection. The page does not mention a phytosanitary certificate or penalties. It describes CITES permits for protected species, and for domestic protected species it says no import permit is needed but you fill in an import notification form at the border. Online purchases go through a customs agent, who asks the plant health inspection whether a permit is needed, which adds cost.
serbia.src: Source read: Carina.rs, Unos bilja (in Serbian). Penalties and certificates are not on the page.

singapore.h: What the National Parks Board of Singapore says about plants and seeds
p: The National Parks Board (NParks) page on importing plants says plants and seeds brought in as a consignment need a phytosanitary certificate from the exporting country's plant protection organisation and then an import permit before they enter Singapore. Seeds must be for sowing, not for eating, and must be free of plant pests, with seeds for planting generally exempt from the additional declarations. Plants with growing medium need a declaration that they are free from plant-parasitic nematodes, or a nematicide treatment endorsed on the certificate.

For travellers there is one allowance: without a certificate or permit, each person may hand-carry from West Malaysia up to 3 non-CITES plants without potting medium and 250 grams of seeds, including plants bought from accredited Malaysian nurseries under the MPCA scheme. Excess quantities, from West Malaysia or elsewhere, may be detained by ICA or Singapore Customs if the papers are missing. The page gives no fines.
singapore.src: Source read: NParks, Ornamental plants, nursery stock and seeds (import requirements). Fines are not on the page.

south-africa.h: What a South African government news item says about plant health permits
p: A South African Government News Agency article of 26 December 2024 says plants and plant products need a plant health import permit, which the Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development issues through its Food Import and Export Standards Directorate. It lists soil and growth medium as prohibited agricultural products that travellers should not bring in.

The article warns that importers and travellers who do not comply risk having their products seized at the port of entry. It is a news item, not the department's own traveller page, so it does not give an allowance for a few seeds or a plant, and it does not describe fines. Ask the department before you bring any plant or seed.
south-africa.src: Source read: SAnews.gov.za, article of 26 December 2024. It is a news item and gives no allowance or fine.

saudi-arabia.h: Saudi Arabia: what the UK government advice says about seeds
p: We re-read the UK government's travel advice for Saudi Arabia. It lists agricultural seeds among the items you may need special approval to bring in, next to live animals, chemicals and harmful materials and some pharmaceutical products. It adds that you must declare anything that may be prohibited or subject to tax or duty, and it advises contacting the Saudi embassy for customs questions.

This is the advice of another country's government, not a Saudi authority, which is why the card is marked unofficial. The page says nothing about live plants, the approval steps or penalties. Ask the Saudi Ministry of Environment, Water and Agriculture before you bring any plant or seed.
saudi-arabia.src: Source read: UK government (FCDO), Saudi Arabia entry requirements. This is an unofficial source and gives no steps or penalties.

seychelles.h: What the Seychelles restricted goods regulations list
p: The Seychelles Customs Management (Prohibited and Restricted Goods) Regulations 2023, published as Statutory Instrument 87, include in their schedule of controlled goods, under the plant and plant products group, live trees and other plants, bulbs, roots and the like, cut flowers and ornamental foliage, edible vegetables and fruit, and name palm plants covered by the Plant Protection (Aleurotrochelus Atratus) Regulations 2007.

We read the schedule as extracted text, which does not show the approving authority or the conditions in each row, so we cannot tell you who approves an import or what is needed. The regulations are a legal text, not a traveller guide. Ask the Seychelles Revenue Commission or the agriculture authority before you bring any plant, bulb or cut flower.
seychelles.src: Source read: Seychelles S.I. 87 of 2023 (Prohibited and Restricted Goods Regulations), as extracted text. The approving authority is not shown in the extract.

south-korea.h: What the Travel Doc customs page says about plants and seeds in South Korea
p: The Travel Doc customs page for South Korea lists agricultural, forest and plant products as restricted, with limits of up to 5 kg of each item and 40 kg in total, within a value of 100,000 won. Restricted goods generally need a permit before arrival. Seeds are not mentioned separately.
The page names no publisher and shows no date, so confirm the figures with the customs authority before you travel.
south-korea.src: Unofficial source, read 16 November 2026: Travel Doc customs information page for South Korea (infopages.traveldoc.aero, undated; it names no publisher). The official customs site could not be read.
link: Travel Doc: South Korea customs information

sri-lanka.h: What the Sri Lankan plant quarantine service says about air passengers
p: The Sri Lankan plant protection service page for air passengers says plants and plant products are prohibited unless you have prior permission, and that violations are punishable under the Plant Protection Act No. 35 of 1999. You need a valid import permit from the National Plant Quarantine Service, along with the required documents.

On arrival you declare all plants and plant products on the customs declaration form and tell the Plant Quarantine Officer at the arrivals terminal. The officer inspects each item, checks the documents and confirms the import conditions before clearance, for a fee of Rs. 150 per consignment. If the officer finds pests, permit violations or false documents, the consignment may be detained and destroyed or sent back. Plants and plant products arriving by mail or courier go through quarantine too.
sri-lanka.src: Source read: Department of Agriculture Sri Lanka, plant quarantine page for air passengers. It does not give a fine amount.

switzerland.h: What the Swiss Federal Office for Agriculture says about importing plants
p: The Swiss Federal Office for Agriculture says that for non-EU countries, imports of plant material such as fruit, vegetables, seedlings, seeds or other fresh plant material must come with a phytosanitary certificate. Pineapples, coconuts, durians, bananas and dates need none, and processed plant products such as dried, powdered, frozen or pickled ones need none and are not inspected, so spices and tea are generally fine. Some plants are prohibited outright, and soil and organic substrate are prohibited, though exemptions may be granted.

If you fly in with plants, you send your flight details to the Swiss plant protection service by email in advance, then at Zurich, Geneva or Basel go through the red door and tell the service. Inspection is free for private individuals. By post or courier the original certificate must be enclosed, issued no more than 14 days before handover, and the fee is CHF 30 for private individuals. Plants in personal luggage need no plant passport, and fruit, vegetables and cut flowers can come from the EU without one. The page sets no quantity limits and describes no penalties.
switzerland.src: Source read: Federal Office for Agriculture (BLW), Importing plants (English). Quantity limits and penalties are not on the page.

thailand.h: What the Suvarnabhumi airport guide says about prohibited plants
p: The Suvarnabhumi Airport guide on plants for import says travellers may not bring in fresh fruit, propagating material such as seeds and cuttings, or soil, organic fertiliser, microorganisms and animal pests from any country. Fresh vegetables, ornamental plants, seeds or grain, and some other products such as dried tea leaves and mushrooms may come in only if declared to a plant quarantine officer, with a phytosanitary certificate, and found free of pests.

The page says importers apply through the National Single Window, and prohibited items need an import permit (Form P.Q. 2-1) and a phytosanitary certificate, with a non-GMO certificate sometimes needed for planting material and a CITES permit for listed items. Section 21 of the Plant Quarantine Act sets a maximum of one year in prison or a fine of up to 20,000 baht, and goods that do not comply are confiscated and destroyed with no refund. The Office of Agricultural Regulation is the contact. The airport guide reproduces the Department of Agriculture rules and is not the department's own page.
thailand.src: Source read: Suvarnabhumi Airport (airportthai.co.th), Prohibited plants for import. It reproduces Department of Agriculture rules.

turkey.h: What a Turkish plant quarantine directorate says about passenger allowances
p: The Hatay Plant Quarantine Directorate of the Turkish agriculture ministry says travellers may carry fresh and dried fruit and vegetables for personal consumption up to three kilograms, and above that the import procedures apply. One flower bouquet and one wreath are allowed for non-commercial purposes, and more than that is also subject to import procedures.

Passengers may not bring any seeds, tubers, seedlings, saplings or cuttings, whatever the quantity. Such items can be imported only under the Plant Quarantine Regulation. This is a regional directorate's page, so check the ministry's current rules, and note that the page lists no penalties.
turkey.src: Source read: T.C. Tarım ve Orman Bakanlığı, Hatay Plant Quarantine Directorate, Passenger allowances (in Turkish). Penalties are not on the page.

united-kingdom.h: What GOV.UK says about plants from outside the EU
p: GOV.UK says plants and plant-based products brought into Great Britain from outside the EU, Switzerland and Liechtenstein need a phytosanitary certificate. The items it names are plants for planting, decorative parts of trees, cut flowers and foliage, and natural, non-manufactured wood. If you bring in more than 2 kg of plants for planting, you must arrange for a plant health inspector to examine them when they enter Great Britain.

The page links to a separate guide on how to get a phytosanitary certificate and to the plant health authority contacts of each country. It does not mention seeds, personal luggage, prohibited items or penalties, so check the other GOV.UK plant health pages before you bring any seeds.
united-kingdom.src: Source read: GOV.UK, Bringing plants and wood into Great Britain from outside the EU. Seeds and penalties are not on the page.

united-states.h: What USDA APHIS says about bringing plants and seeds
p: The U.S. Department of Agriculture's plant health service APHIS says you must declare all agricultural or wildlife products to Customs and Border Protection and say whether you visited a farm or had contact with animals before you arrived. Keep receipts and original packaging. If you declare everything you will not face penalties, even if an inspector refuses entry to an item. Plants growing in soil are prohibited, and so are seeds from trees and shrubs in passenger baggage.

You may bring up to 12 bare-root plants with no soil or growing medium if they are not otherwise prohibited or protected, you have a phytosanitary certificate from the exporting country, and CBP clears them at the first port of entry. Seeds of admissible herbaceous plants have the same conditions. Thirteen or more plants need an APHIS import permit, which can take up to 30 business days, and the plants must be shipped to a USDA Plant Inspection Station. Fresh cut flowers must be presented to CBP at the first port of entry. The APHIS import information line is 877-770-5990.
united-states.src: Source read: USDA APHIS, Plants and plant parts (traveling with ag products). Penalties for not declaring are not stated beyond the declared-items note.

vietnam.h: What the Vietnamese plant protection and quarantine law says about luggage
p: We read the English text of Law No. 41/2013/QH13 on plant protection and quarantine, passed on 25 November 2013, on a legal database site. Article 29 says quarantine-liable plant articles that travellers carry in hand luggage, or that are consigned with carriers, must be declared and inspected under rules set by the Minister of Agriculture and Rural Development, and that goods may clear customs only after all import quarantine procedures are done. Article 26 requires a phytosanitary certificate from the exporting country and no listed quarantine pests.

Article 13 bans importing infested plants that have not been treated and carrying soil or harmful organisms unless the Minister approves in writing. We read the first part of a long text, and it states no fines for luggage violations. It is an unofficial English translation on a commercial site, which is why the card is marked unofficial, and it is a law from 2013, so check Vietnamese plant quarantine rules before you travel.
vietnam.src: Source read: English text of Law No. 41/2013/QH13 on luatvietnam.vn, first 100,000 characters. It is an unofficial translation and gives no fines for luggage.

united-arab-emirates.h: What the Dubai Customs passenger guide says about seedlings
p: The Dubai Customs passenger guide lists plants and seedlings among goods in a table of controlled categories, next to items such as drones, food products and filming equipment, and says separately that agricultural seedlings containing soil are not allowed to be brought in by a traveller.

We read the guide as extracted text, and the table does not clearly show which authority's permit each category needs, so we cannot state the permit steps. The guide does not set an allowance for a few seeds or a plant and gives no penalty for plants. Ask the UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment before you bring any plant or seed.
united-arab-emirates.src: Source read: Dubai Customs, Passenger customs guide (PDF, extracted text). Permit steps and penalties are not stated.

ukraine.h: What the Ukrainian plant quarantine law says about baggage checks
p: We read an English translation of Ukraine's law on plant quarantine, held in the VERTIC national legislation library. It says the border, oblast and city inspections on plant quarantine conduct quarantine checks and laboratory examination of materials and objects subject to quarantine delivered from abroad, including those delivered in baggage, postal correspondence and passenger hand luggage. It also gives the State Service on Plant Quarantine the power to set the procedure for bringing seed, plants and plant products in from abroad.

The law is a general framework from the 1990s, so it does not list what a traveller may carry, give an allowance or set fines, and the rules may have changed since. The translation is held on a third-party site, which is why the card is marked unofficial. Check the State Service of Ukraine on Food Safety and Consumer Protection before you bring any plant or seed.
ukraine.src: Source read: Law of Ukraine on Plant Quarantine (English translation, VERTIC library). It is an old framework law with no traveller list or fines.

taiwan.h: Plants and seeds in Taiwan: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says passengers cannot bring any fresh fruit from any country into Taiwan, and that live plants, seeds, bulbs and soil must go through plant quarantine. It comes from the English page of the Bureau of Animal and Plant Health Inspection and Quarantine that we link below the card.

We could not re-open the official page, so we checked the UK government's travel advice for Taiwan, an unofficial source. On food and plants it says not to bring animal products without authorisation. It says nothing about live plants or seeds, so the general rule applies there: most countries ask for a plant health certificate from the country of origin for plants and seeds, ban soil, and seize or destroy plants that arrive without papers. We could not confirm more for Taiwan, so ask the Taiwanese Customs Administration before you bring any plant or seed.
taiwan.src: UK government (FCDO) entry requirements page, read 16 November 2026. It is an unofficial source: it is another country's travel advice.

spain.h: What the Spanish Tax Agency says about plants and seeds in luggage
p: The Spanish Tax Agency (AEAT) says plants, plant products and vegetables in luggage from third countries need an official phytosanitary certificate from the country of origin, unless exempt. Coconut, date, durian, banana and pineapple need none. Live plants, including bonsai and propagation material such as cuttings and grafts, must be declared whatever the quantity or personal use, and must be free of soil. Potatoes and tubers must always be declared at customs, whatever the weight.

Live plants, potatoes and other tubers can enter only through border control posts, after inspection by the plant health inspection service. Items in Annex VI of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072 are banned from the EU. The Canary Islands, Ceuta and Melilla have special rules, for example fruit and vegetables for personal use in Ceuta and Melilla may go undeclared. The page does not mention seeds specifically and describes no penalties. For details it names the plant health inspection service of the government delegations.

The Spanish Ministry of Agriculture (MAPA) traveller page adds that the rules also apply if you reach Spain indirectly from another EU country but the goods come from a non-EU country. Seeds, wood, live plants, fruit, vegetables and flowers in your luggage need an official phytosanitary certificate from the country of origin, except coconut, date, durian, banana and pineapple. Live plants, bonsai and cuttings or grafts must be declared at Spanish customs for personal use and whatever the quantity, and must be free of soil. For the Canary Islands, the page says goods in Annex III of a 1987 Ministry order cannot be brought in at all, and Annex V goods only if declared at destination customs, with a certificate and free of soil. For Ceuta and Melilla, fruit and vegetables for your own use that are not a commercial shipment need not be declared.
spain.src: Source read: Agencia Tributaria, Semillas, plantas y vegetales (in Spanish). Seeds and penalties are not on the page. Also read 23 November 2026: Ministerio de Agricultura, Pesca y Alimentación, "Información para viajeros para introducción de vegetales y productos vegetales" (mapa.gob.es, in Spanish).

sweden.h: What the Swedish Board of Agriculture says about plants for private persons
p: The Swedish Board of Agriculture (Jordbruksverket) says that within the EU, personal purchases of plants or plant products generally need no health certificate, though quarantine pests must never be spread. From outside the EU, most plants for planting and many plant products need a phytosanitary certificate from the exporting country's plant health authority, usually paid for by the traveller, with exemptions for Switzerland, Liechtenstein and Northern Ireland. Fresh pineapple, banana, coconut, date and durian are exempt, as are dried seeds not meant for sowing, dried and frozen produce and processed foods.

Some items cannot be brought in at all from outside the EU, including many conifer seedlings, citrus plants and seed potatoes. The Board inspects regulated plants and seeds at a Swedish border checkpoint or the first EU country they reach, for a fee, and you request the inspection form by email to importkontroll@jordbruksverket.se. Seeds for sowing are inspected if they are on the EU list. Endangered plants fall under CITES permits. The page does not cover soil or penalties.
sweden.src: Source read: Jordbruksverket, Ta med eller beställa växter och växtprodukter till Sverige som privatperson (in Swedish). Soil and penalties are not on the page.

slovakia.h: What the Slovak Financial Administration says about non-commercial plant imports
p: The Finančná správa (customs) page on non-commercial plant imports cites Act 405/2011 on plant health and Government Regulation 199/2005. It says the plant health rules allow a small amount of plants, plant products, food or feed to be carried into the EU when it is meant for use during the journey and by the owner or recipient, not for industry, trials, science or breeding, and when it poses no risk of spreading harmful organisms. In the same passage it says every consignment of plants and plant products must come with a phytosanitary certificate from the country of origin and is subject to plant health control on import.

It then lists the only items that need no certificate under Regulation (EU) 2019/2072: pineapples, coconuts, durians, bananas (including plantains) and dates, fresh or dried, from all third countries. For anything else it refers to the Central Control and Testing Institute in Agriculture (ÚKSÚP). The same page says customs offences by individuals can bring a reprimand, a fine or forfeiture of the goods, with fines of up to EUR 3,319.39; it does not say which fine applies to plants or seeds.
slovakia.src: Source read on 22 November 2026: Finančná správa (financnasprava.sk), Zákazy a obmedzenia, section "Dovoz rastlinného tovaru neobchodného charakteru" (in Slovak). A seed-specific rule is not on the page.

slovenia.h: What the Slovenian food safety and plant protection administration says
p: The Administration of the Republic of Slovenia for Food Safety, Veterinary Sector and Plant Protection, under the Ministry of Agriculture, lists what counts as a plant in a traveller's bag: fruit, vegetables, potted plants, perennial seedlings, grafts, substrates, sowing material, cut flowers, branches and other plant parts, plus plant products such as dried grains and wood.

It says these can bring in harmful organisms, so some are banned from the EU altogether, and for most of the others import is allowed only with a phytosanitary certificate and after a phytosanitary inspection on prior notification. The page is marked as still under construction and gives no quantity limits, no fee and no separate seed rule.

The Financial Administration (customs, FURS) page "Import of plants and plant products" gives the numbers. Small quantities from European countries need no inspection: fruit and raw vegetables 5 kg (not potatoes), seeds in original packaging not for sale 0.5 kg, flower bulbs and tubers 5 kg, one bouquet or wreath, one rootless Christmas tree, 3 indoor pot plants (not bonsai), 10 balcony plants or unlignified ornamental shrubs. Anything above that, or not banned, must be declared at the first EU entry point with a phytosanitary certificate from the country of origin; in Slovenia that means Port Koper, Ljubljana Jože Pučnik Airport or the Ljubljana customs post office (internet purchases).

Banned even in small amounts: potatoes, vines, citrus plants, bonsai and non-ornamental grasses. From the USA, Canada and China, plants with a root clod, conifers, chestnut, oak, apple, quince, pear, cherry, plum and other stone-fruit trees and roses are also banned.
slovenia.src: Source read on 22 November 2026: gov.si, Introduction of personal consignments of plants and products of animal and plant origin. The page says it is under construction. Also read on 24 November 2026: fu.gov.si, Import of plants and plant products (page refreshed 26 October 2022).

romania.h: What the Romanian plant health authority (ANF) says about border checks
p: The Autoritatea Națională Fitosanitară (ANF) states in a press release dated 3 March 2023 that its inspectors check seeds, plants and plant products intended for planting at border control points. Cereals and other plant products meant for eating or processing are checked by the food safety and veterinary authority (ANSVSA) instead, because EU rules treat them as no phytosanitary risk to crops.

For the list of plants and products that need a phytosanitary certificate, ANF points to Annex XI, Parts A and B of Regulation (EU) 2019/2072, and to Annex VII for the special entry conditions. The release speaks about border controls in general; it does not give a traveller allowance, a seed quantity or a fine.
