ANF's article "Ce plante nu puteți aduce în bagaj la intrarea în UE" (3 November 2026) answers the traveller question directly: since 14 December 2019 there is no small-quantity or personal-use exemption, so almost any plant, fruit or seed from outside the EU needs a phytosanitary certificate from the country of origin. Only five fruits are exempt, from all non-EU countries: pineapple, coconut, banana (including plantain), dates, and durian (fresh only; dried durian still needs a certificate).

It adds that the luggage exemption in Regulation 2019/2122 covers only the border-post check, not the certificate, and that planting material (seeds for sowing, seedlings, bulbs) still goes through a border control post with inspection. Non-conforming goods found are confiscated and destroyed, and the traveller can also be fined. Between EU countries no certificate is needed, and a plant bought in another member state for your own garden needs no plant passport, but an online order of passport-category plants does.
romania.src: Source read on 22 November 2026: ANF press release "Comunicat de presă" of 3 March 2023 (anfdf.ro, in Romanian). It does not address luggage allowances. Also read on 24 November 2026: anfdf.ro, "Ce plante nu puteți aduce în bagaj la intrarea în UE", 3 November 2026.

argentina.h: How the Argentine customs declaration treats cash
p: Argentina's customs service, ARCA, names three situations in which an arriving traveller must hand in the customs declaration. One of them is bringing cash or monetary instruments, in foreign or Argentine legal currency, worth the equivalent of US$10,000 or more. The other two are owing duty because you went over your allowance and carrying goods regulated by SENASA.

The declaration is made preferably on the digital arrival baggage form, available in mobile apps and on self-service terminals. A traveller who cannot do it digitally uses the manual form OM-2087/G5 or OM-2087/G6, whichever applies. The page we read does not describe penalties for failing to declare money, so we cannot state any here.
argentina.src: Source read: ARCA, Viajeros: régimen de equipaje. It does not mention cash on departure or fines.

austria.h: How the Austrian Ministry of Finance explains carrying cash
p: The Austrian Ministry of Finance (BMF) says that anyone crossing the EU's external border by air, land, rail or sea with EUR 10,000 or more must declare it, whether entering or leaving the EU. The rule counts the equivalent in other currencies and easily convertible values such as cheques, and it applies to each person in a group separately, so a family cannot add its money together to stay under the limit.

Cash here means banknotes and coins, including withdrawn currencies a bank can still exchange, bearer instruments such as cheques, traveller's cheques and promissory notes, gold coins with at least 90% gold content and gold bars or nuggets with at least 99.5%. Casino chips do not count. For minors the declaration is made through a parent or legal guardian. Customs may check people, luggage and vehicles, may hold undeclared cash, and can act on smaller amounts if there are signs of a link to crime. The EU rules in force since 3 June 2021 come from Regulation 2018/1672.
austria.src: Source read: BMF, Mitnahme von Bargeld (first part of the page). We did not read the forms page or the penalty details.

brazil.h: What the Receita Federal says about cash on entry
p: Brazil's tax and customs authority, the Receita Federal, requires every traveller entering Brazil with more than US$10,000, or the equivalent in another currency, to fill in the e-DBV, the electronic declaration of travellers' goods, and present it at customs inspection. The wording is "more than" US$10,000, which differs from the "10,000 or more" used by Argentina and the EU.

The page says the declaration covers physical banknotes, Brazilian or foreign, and that securities, cheques and traveller's cheques are not included. You complete the e-DBV online and present it, with the total amount you carry, in the travellers' goods control area on arrival before leaving the customs area. The page does not describe penalties and points to the legislation it cites, so ask the Receita Federal about a specific case.
brazil.src: Source read: Receita Federal, dinheiro em espécie (cash on entry). Penalties are not described on the page.

australia.h: Cash in Australia: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card states that A$10,000 or more, or the foreign equivalent, must be declared when entering or leaving Australia, and that not declaring can mean penalties. That is the rule from the Australian Border Force and AUSTRAC pages we link below the card.

The official page could not be re-opened, and the UK government's travel advice for Australia, which we also read, says nothing about cash. So this section applies the general rule most countries follow: the usual pattern worldwide is that cash is legal to carry, a declaration starts at a threshold, and not declaring risks seizure. For Australia we have the card figure only, so use the Australian Border Force as the place to confirm it.
australia.src: Official page not re-opened; the UK government (FCDO) advice read on 16 November 2026 does not cover cash. Global rule applied, unofficial.

bahrain.h: What the Travel Doc customs page says about cash in Bahrain
p: The Travel Doc customs page for Bahrain states there are no import restrictions on local or foreign currency.
The page names no publisher and shows no date, so confirm the figures with the customs authority before you travel.
bahrain.src: Unofficial source, read 16 November 2026: Travel Doc customs information page for Bahrain (infopages.traveldoc.aero, undated; it names no publisher). The official customs site could not be read.

belgium.h: Cash in Belgium: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card gives the EU rule: declare EUR 10,000 or more in cash, or the equivalent, when entering or leaving the EU, and not declaring can mean penalties. The EU Your Europe page we link below the card adds that there are no EU-wide rules for cash moved between EU countries, so check with the customs of the countries you leave and enter.

We could not re-open the official page, so we checked the UK government's travel advice for Belgium, an unofficial source. On cash it says to complete a disclosure form at customs for currency worth 10,000 euros or more. Carrying money across a border is never banned by itself, but a large amount without a declaration is the single most common reason cash is seized. For Belgium, the figure on the card is what to follow, and Belgian Customs and Excise can confirm it.
belgium.src: UK government (FCDO) entry requirements page, read 16 November 2026. It is an unofficial source: it is another country's travel advice.

cambodia.h: What the Cambodian tourism authority says about carrying currency
p: The Ministry of Tourism's customs and excise page says importing foreign currency into Cambodia is not limited, but a declaration is required for sums of over US$10,000. Taking foreign currency out is stricter: an amount above US$10,000 needs a permit from the National Bank of Cambodia, and the page ties this to the case where there was no import declaration of the currency at entry. Approval from the General Department of Customs and Excise is also mentioned.

The page does not name the form for the cash declaration and lists no currency-specific penalty. It does say that passengers face prosecution or penalties for false declarations. It also separates the green channel, for travellers with nothing to declare, from the red channel for dutiable, restricted or prohibited goods, and warns that random checks happen in both.
cambodia.src: Source read: Cambodia Ministry of Tourism, customs and excise page. It names no cash form and no cash penalty.

canada.h: How the CBSA handles C$10,000 or more
p: The Canada Border Services Agency says there is no limit on the money you can bring into or take out of Canada, but currency or monetary instruments worth C$10,000 or more, in Canadian or foreign money or both, must be reported. Monetary instruments include stocks and bonds, cheques, money orders, bank drafts and traveller's cheques. You report your own money on form E677 and money for someone else on form E667; on arrival you can report at an airport kiosk, on the declaration card, in an advance declaration, or verbally to an officer.

Leaving Canada by air, you report at a CBSA office on the arrivals level before the security screening area, and the page says NEXUS cannot be used when crossing with C$10,000 or more. If the amount is not fully reported, the CBSA can seize it, and funds may be returned after a penalty of 5% to 50% of the amount seized; funds suspected to be crime or terrorist financing are not returned. A seizure can be disputed by filing a review.
canada.src: Source read: CBSA, travelling with CAN$10,000 or more.

chile.h: What Chilean Customs says about money you carry
p: The traveller FAQ of the Chilean Customs Service answers the question "must I declare the money I carry?" The rule is that anyone entering Chile with cash or negotiable instruments above US$10,000, or the equivalent in other currencies including Chilean pesos, must declare them. The wording is "above" US$10,000, so exactly 10,000 is not covered by this page's text.

To declare, the traveller goes to a customs officer on arrival and completes the declaration form. The page cites the Compendium of Customs Norms (Chapter III, 17.10.1 and 17.10.3), Annex 59 and Resolution 003816 of 2001 as the basis. The part of the page we could read does not state penalties for failing to declare.
chile.src: Source read: Aduanas de Chile, traveller FAQ (most of the page; the last part was not read). No penalties stated.

china.h: What China Customs says about cash in its passenger guide
p: China Customs lists RMB 20,000 in cash or more, or foreign currency in cash equivalent to US$5,000 or more, among the items for which an inward passenger must choose the red channel, the goods-to-declare lane. The guide says such items are dealt with according to the current regulations.

It adds a practical step for foreign cash: a passenger carrying more than US$5,000 who intends to take the currency out of China later must fill out two declaration forms. After the customs endorsement one copy is returned to the passenger, to be shown when leaving China. The guide does not give penalties. Our reading of this page needed a connection that skips the site's certificate check, which is another reason to confirm the current rule with China Customs before you travel.
china.src: Source read: China Customs, clearance guide for international passengers.

colombia.h: What DIAN says about Form 530 and cash
p: Colombia's tax and customs authority, DIAN, says a traveller entering with more than US$10,000, or the equivalent in other currencies, must file Form 530. It covers cash in any currency, including Colombian pesos, and securities that represent money. On entry the form is completed on arrival at the first port, airport or border crossing; on leaving it is completed after immigration, even if the trip does not take place.

Form 530 is also required for other cases, for example baggage subject to the single tax, goods in commercial quantities, vegetables, animals and pets, and cultural heritage items. International airlines must provide the form, and at land and sea crossings it is at the customs control post. The page says undeclared baggage subject to the single tax is seized and forfeited, and it gives no money fine for undeclared cash.
colombia.src: Source read: DIAN, Declaración de viajeros, Formulario 530. The English and Spanish versions differ on some other triggers.

bulgaria.h: What the Bulgarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs says about cash
p: The Bulgarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs says that since 15 July 2007 every EU member state has applied the cash-movement rule: passengers with 10,000 euros or more, or the equivalent in other currencies and cheques, declare it to customs when entering or leaving the country. Customs may check the luggage and take undeclared amounts.

It recommends filling in the declaration in advance rather than during the customs check, and says customs officers will help with the form. Parliament passed an amendment to the Currency Act in September 2023, reported by the Bulgarian News Agency, covering cash of 10,000 euros or more crossing the border to or from a third country.
The UK government's travel advice for Bulgaria adds that you should get a certified declaration, or the money could be seized when you leave.
bulgaria.src: Official source read 23 November 2026: Bulgarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, "Declaring cash" (mfa.bg). The 2023 amendment is from the Bulgarian News Agency (BTA, 18 September 2023); the certified-declaration advice is from the UK FCDO, an unofficial source.
link: Bulgarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs: Declaring cash

croatia.h: What Croatian Customs says about carrying cash
p: The Croatian Customs Administration says moving cash is free and has no amount limit, and that the only requirement is a declaration: EUR 10,000 or more, or the equivalent, when entering or leaving the EU must be declared to a customs officer at the border customs office. It counts banknotes and coins, cheques, traveller's cheques, promissory notes and payment orders with no named payee, gold coins with at least 90% gold, gold bars, grains or nuggets with at least 99.5% gold, and prepaid cards.

Travellers use the cash declaration form, HR1 in Croatian or EN1 in English. You can fill it in electronically and email it to operativno@carina.hr, print it and hand it to the officer, or complete it at the border office. Croatia also has a national control for movements to or from another EU country: when a customs or border police officer asks, a person carrying EUR 10,000 or more must declare it in writing on the Article 24 form (HR5 or EN5). The page does not describe penalties.
croatia.src: Source read: Carinska uprava, Unos i iznos novca (rules from 26 March 2026). No penalties stated on the page.

czechia.h: What the Czech Customs Administration says about cash
p: The Czech Customs Administration checks compliance with sections 41 and 41a of Act No. 253/2008 and the EU cash-control regulation. Under section 41, a person entering the Czech Republic from outside the EU, or leaving it for outside the EU, must declare in writing cash of at least EUR 10,000, on the common EU form available on the customs website or at the office. A cumulative rule applies: if you know you will reach EUR 10,000 moved into or out of the EU within 12 consecutive months, the duty arises at that point.

Section 41a adds an information duty that applies on request: a person carrying at least EUR 15,000 must tell customs about the identity of the owner and recipient, the type, value and origin of the cash and its purpose, which also covers movements between the Czech Republic and another EU state. Foreign currency is converted at the Czech National Bank rate for the penultimate Wednesday of the month before the duty arises. Customs may seize cash it suspects is linked to a breach or to money laundering, and the page says fines can reach CZK 10,000,000.
czechia.src: Source read: Celní správa ČR, Kontrola hotovosti. The page does not make clear whether the 12-month rule also covers moves inside the EU.

denmark.h: What Toldstyrelsen says about travelling with EUR 10,000 or more
p: The Danish Customs Authority, Toldstyrelsen, says cash or other liquid assets worth EUR 10,000 (about DKK 75,000) or more must be declared when entering or leaving Denmark, in any currency and whether you travel privately or for a company. The duty applies even if you only pass through Denmark, for example by car or train. Liquid assets include cash, travellers' cheques and other cheques, gold coins with at least 90% gold and bars or nuggets with at least 99.5% gold.

You complete a declaration form either in advance or at the customs point. There are two online forms, one that needs MitID login and one that does not, and even after filling it in beforehand you must visit a customs point at the airport or crossing and note your reference number. Customs may examine and detain amounts below the threshold too if there are signs of a link to crime, and not declaring can mean a fine and seizure of the valuables.
denmark.src: Source read: Toldstyrelsen, store værdier (travelling with large amounts).

cyprus.h: What the Cyprus Department of Customs says about cash
p: The Cyprus Customs and Excise page on cash control says anyone carrying cash of EUR 10,000 or more must declare it in writing. Unlike the EU border rule on many other pages, it applies to a natural person entering the Republic of Cyprus from a third country or from another member state, and it also covers people leaving. The declaration goes to Customs at the control point where you enter or leave.

Cash for this purpose includes currency, bearer-negotiable instruments, coins with at least 90% gold content and bullion such as bars, nuggets or clumps with at least 99.5% gold. For unaccompanied cash, Customs may ask the sender, recipient or their representative for a disclosure declaration within 30 days. Failing to declare, or filing an incomplete or false declaration, is an offence: the page lists arrest, seizure of the cash, and liability to up to three years in prison or a fine of up to EUR 100,000, which the Director of Customs and Excise can compound.
cyprus.src: Source read: Cyprus Customs and Excise, cash control page. Contact given on the page: headquarters@customs.mof.gov.cy.

costa-rica.h: Cash in Costa Rica: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says travellers must declare cash worth US$10,000 or more, and securities worth US$50,000 or more, on the customs declaration, and that undeclared money above the limits is held by customs. It comes from the AduanaFácil page of the Ministry of Finance that we link below the card.

We could not re-open the official page, so we checked the UK government's travel advice for Costa Rica, an unofficial source. On cash it says to declare cash, travellers' cheques or goods worth 10,000 US dollars or more, get a certified declaration, and warns that without it money or goods could be seized when you leave. In practice, a traveller who carries more than the threshold fills in a short form at the border, shows the money if asked, and gets a stamped copy to prove it was declared. Costa Rica's threshold is on the card; the Dirección General de Aduanas holds the form.
costa-rica.src: UK government (FCDO) entry requirements page, read 16 November 2026. It is an unofficial source: it is another country's travel advice.

cuba.h: Cash in Cuba: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says there is no limit on the convertible currency a private traveller may bring in, in cash, cheques or other bank payment instruments, and that more than US$5,000, or the equivalent, must be declared on the Customs Declaration for Passengers, which must always be filled in. It comes from the FAQ of Cuban Customs that we link below the card.

We could not re-open the official page, so we checked the UK government's travel advice for Cuba, an unofficial source. On cash it says to declare foreign currency worth more than 5,000 US dollars, and adds that the Cuban peso cannot be exchanged outside Cuba and that money may be exchanged only at Cadeca exchange houses. Carrying money across a border is never banned by itself, but a large amount without a declaration is the single most common reason cash is seized. For Cuba, the figure on the card is what to follow, and the Cuban customs service (Aduana General) can confirm it.
cuba.src: UK government (FCDO) entry requirements page, read 16 November 2026. It is an unofficial source: it is another country's travel advice.

dominican-republic.h: What the Dominican customs traveller manual says about cash
p: The Dirección General de Aduanas (DGA) traveller manual says cash of US$10,000 or its equivalent in Dominican pesos or another currency must be declared, and so must bearer securities. The duty applies both when you enter and when you leave the country, and the declaration is made to DGA officials on the form the DGA has enabled for this. The page does not name or link the form.

You must also present documents that show the lawful origin of the money. The manual says no tax is charged for carrying money, so the point of the rule is the declaration, not a duty. One FAQ on the page words the threshold as 'more than' US$10,000, so a traveller carrying exactly that amount should declare it to be safe. The page does not list penalties.
dominican-republic.src: Source read: DGA, Manual del Viajero. Penalties and the form name are not on the page.

egypt.h: Cash in Egypt: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says you can bring up to 5,000 Egyptian pounds into or out of Egypt, that foreign currency worth more than US$10,000 must be declared on arrival, and that there is no limit on the foreign currency you can bring. That comes from the UK government's Egypt travel advice, an unofficial source for Egypt itself.

We could not re-open the official page, so we checked the UK government's travel advice for Egypt, an unofficial source. On cash it says that you can bring up to 5,000 Egyptian pounds in or out and must declare foreign currency above 10,000 US dollars on arrival, with no limit on the amount of foreign currency. Border cash rules follow one common idea: you may bring money, but large sums must be declared, and a missing declaration can cost you the money. Check the Egyptian Customs Authority for the current Egypt threshold and the form.
egypt.src: UK government (FCDO) entry requirements page, read 16 November 2026. It is an unofficial source: it is another country's travel advice.

estonia.h: What the Estonian Tax and Customs Board says about cash
p: The Estonian Tax and Customs Board (EMTA) says anyone entering or leaving the EU with EUR 10,000 or more must declare it. Cash covers banknotes and coins in any currency, including ones no longer in circulation, bearer-negotiable instruments such as traveller's cheques and promissory notes, coins with at least 90% gold and gold nuggets or clumps with at least 99.5% gold. Customs may also check smaller amounts if there is information linking the cash to crime.

The preferred route is the e-MTA portal, under Customs, Simplified declarations, Cash declaration, up to three days before you cross. At the border you take the red lane and tell the officer you have filed. The page says the online webform was unavailable when we read it, in which case you contact a customs officer. Use the exchange rate from the day before you submit.

Separate rules apply to Russia and Belarus: euro banknotes and other EU-currency banknotes may not be exported there except for personal use by the traveller or accompanying family, with no fixed amount but a duty to justify it. The page does not list penalties for failing to declare.
estonia.src: Source read: EMTA, Declaration of cash. Penalties for non-declaration are not stated on the page.

ethiopia.h: Cash in Ethiopia: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says passengers may carry up to 3,000 birr per trip in or out, that foreign currency above US$10,000 (or the equivalent) needs a customs declaration, and that non-residents may hold foreign currency while their visa is valid. It comes from Ethiopian Airlines' notice about the National Bank of Ethiopia directive.

We could not re-open the official page, so we checked the UK government's travel advice for Ethiopia, an unofficial source. On cash it says that you may carry up to 3,000 birr in or out (10,000 for Djibouti), that over-limit amounts can be seized, that any cash over 10,000 US dollars must be declared, that residents declare over 4,000 US dollars and land-border travellers over 500 US dollars. Most countries let you carry any amount of cash but ask you to declare it above a set threshold, often between about US$5,000 and US$15,000, and undeclared money can be seized and fined. We could not confirm Ethiopia's exact figure beyond the card, so treat the card figure as the one to plan on.
ethiopia.src: UK government (FCDO) entry requirements page, read 16 November 2026. It is an unofficial source: it is another country's travel advice.

fiji.h: What the Fiji Financial Intelligence Unit says about carrying currency
p: The Fiji Financial Intelligence Unit says anyone travelling into or out of Fiji with FJD 10,000 or more, or the equivalent in foreign currency, must declare it. The rule covers currency and bearer negotiable instruments, whether carried on the person or in their belongings.

You declare to Customs officials at the border by completing a Border Currency Reporting Form, which is available at the Customs counters at ports and airports. The page names section 32 of the Financial Transactions Reporting Act as the legal basis. It does not state penalties.
fiji.src: Source read: Fiji FIU, Currency Declaration Rules for Travelers. Penalties are not stated on the page.

finland.h: What Finnish Customs says about cash, on Suomi.fi
p: The Finnish government portal Suomi.fi, describing the Finnish Customs service, says that with over 10,000 euros, or the equivalent in another currency, when entering or leaving the EU you must declare the cash to Customs. Cash means banknotes and coins, other means of payment such as cheques and negotiable promissory notes, gold coins of at least 90% gold, and gold pieces, bars and blocks of at least 99.5% gold. Credit and debit cards do not count.

You declare on a printable Finnish Customs form (PDF): print and fill it in before you travel, attach a copy of your passport or ID, and hand it in on arrival or departure. On arrival choose the red channel or declare to Customs in another way. The portal lists 18 Customs service points, such as the one at Olympia Terminal in Helsinki. The EU wording elsewhere on this site says 10,000 euros or more, so declare if you carry exactly 10,000.
finland.src: Official source read 23 November 2026: Suomi.fi, "Declaring cash when travelling to or from EU nations" and the Finnish Customs cash webpage entry (Finnish Customs, updated 28 January 2026). tulli.fi itself could not be opened.
link: Suomi.fi: Declaring cash when travelling to or from EU nations (Finnish Customs)

france.h: What French Customs says about travelling with EUR 10,000 or more
p: French Customs (DGDDI) says moving cash of EUR 10,000 or more into or out of France must be declared. Cash here means banknotes and coins, bearer negotiable instruments, gold and prepaid cards. The page lists separate online routes for travel to or from another EU country and for travel to or from a non-EU country, and the same EUR 10,000 threshold applies to both.

You declare online through the DALIA service, up to 30 days before the trip, and no handwritten form is needed any more. If you are checked, you show the DALIA declaration on your phone or as a printout. You can create an account, linked to an email address or FranceConnect, to keep your declarations. The page cites articles L222-1 to L222-9 of the Customs Code and says not declaring is a customs offence that can bring a fine and seizure of the money.
france.src: Source read: douane.gouv.fr, Vous voyagez avec 10 000 euros ou plus. The page does not say how much the fine is.

germany.h: What German Customs (Zoll) says about cash
p: The German customs page for travellers leaving for a non-EU country says cash and other means of payment worth EUR 10,000 or more must be declared. It counts valid and still-exchangeable banknotes and coins, bills of exchange, cheques, traveller's cheques, shares and payment orders, gold coins with at least 90% gold and unminted gold with at least 99.5%. Foreign currency is converted at the rate on the day you leave.

The preferred route is the Zoll-Portal service Barmittelanmeldeerklärung, which gives you an identification code to state or show during the trip. Paper forms 040000 (German) and 040001 (English) are accepted in limited cases and must be signed. By air, you hand in the declaration before the security check, and you must declare on your own even if nobody asks. Savings books, gemstones, lower-grade gold and other precious metals have no threshold but must be mentioned if officers ask.

Not declaring, or declaring wrongly or incompletely, is an administrative offence with a fine of up to EUR 1 million, and a person with no home in Germany must also deposit a security amount. This page covers leaving Germany only. It does not describe travel within the EU.
germany.src: Source read: zoll.de, Barmittel (travelling to a non-EU country). The page about arriving in Germany was not read.

hungary.h: What the Hungarian customs authority says about declaring cash
p: The Hungarian National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) says cash of EUR 10,000 or more, or the equivalent in another currency, must be declared. There is no upper limit on how much you may carry. The duty applies both entering and leaving the EU, at the external border; if you cross elsewhere, you declare to the customs authority of the country where you enter or leave.

Cash includes banknotes and coins, including ones no longer in circulation but still exchangeable, cheques, traveller's cheques, promissory notes or payment orders without a named payee, prepaid cards not tied to a bank account, gold coins and bars with at least 90% gold and gold particles with at least 99.5%. You fill in the written EU form at the customs office where you cross, and show the cash and the form to the officers. If you do not declare, NAV may impose an administrative fine or hold the cash. The page does not set a declaration rule for moves between EU states and tells you to check with the country concerned.
hungary.src: Source read: NAV, Declaring cash (English). The fine amounts are not on the page.

hong-kong.h: What Hong Kong Customs says about currency and bearer instruments
p: Hong Kong Customs and Excise says travellers arriving at a specified control point with currency and bearer negotiable instruments worth more than HK$120,000 in total must declare them to a Customs officer through the Red Channel. These include banknotes and coins from anywhere, and bearer instruments such as traveller's cheques, bearer cheques, promissory notes, bearer bonds, money orders and postal orders. Foreign money is declared in its original currency and valued at a bank counter selling rate.

You can pre-fill the online E-Form for passengers and show the QR code, or use the paper form in the Red Channel area. People who arrive elsewhere, such as cruise passengers at an anchorage, disclose if asked, and an adult must declare for a child under 16 whom they know is carrying a large amount. People leaving disclose only when an officer asks, and must then declare. Transit passengers at the airport who do not pass immigration are exempt.

For a first breach with no prior money laundering conviction and no suspicion that the money is criminal, the page allows a HK$2,000 payment to settle it. Other cases face prosecution, with a fine of up to HK$500,000 and two years in prison.
hong-kong.src: Source read: Hong Kong Customs and Excise Department, Declaration and Disclosure Requirements.

georgia.h: What the Georgian Revenue Service brochure says about cash
p: A Georgian Revenue Service customs brochure on exemptions from duties and declaring lists cash among the items that cannot go through without declaring: the national or a foreign currency, cheques and securities with a total of more than GEL 30,000, or the equivalent in another currency, when imported or exported.

The brochure we read gives the threshold only. It does not describe the form, the procedure at the border or the penalty, and we do not fill that gap from search results. For how to declare and what happens if you do not, check the Revenue Service (rs.ge) or ask customs at the border before you carry a large amount.
georgia.src: Source read: rs.ge, Exemption of goods from duties and declaring (brochure). Form, procedure and penalty are not in it.

greece.h: What the Greek customs authority (AADE) says about cash
p: The AADE Cash Declaration page says the electronic cash declaration applies to every person entering or leaving the European Union via Greece with EUR 10,000 or more in cash. It is submitted through an online application on the AADE site, with user manuals and a list of frequently asked questions.

One exception is stated: the declaration for unaccompanied cash is still submitted in handwritten form, and electronic submission for that category is announced for the future. The page names Decision 3039 of 28 July 2025 and Regulation (EU) 2018/1672 as the legal basis. It gives no penalty.
greece.src: Source read on 22 November 2026: AADE (Independent Authority for Public Revenue), Cash Declaration (aade.gr/en/liquid-assets-declaration).

iceland.h: What Icelandic Customs (Skatturinn) says about cash
p: Skatturinn, the Icelandic tax and customs authority, says you must declare cash of more than EUR 10,000, or the equivalent in other currencies, when you arrive in or leave Iceland. The rule covers cash, traveller's cheques and bearer negotiable instruments, and it is there to fight money laundering and other cross-border crime.

You fill in the declaration form online (form TS-E29), print it and give it to a customs officer on arrival or departure. Paper forms are also available at the red customs gate. The page lists no fines. It says customs officers may seize valuables they suspect are used in offences under the General Penal Code, citing Customs Law No. 88/2005, Article 162, and that such cases go to the police. It does not say how the rule applies to unaccompanied cash.
iceland.src: Source read: Skatturinn, Cash declaration. Fines are not stated on the page.

india.h: What the Indian customs passenger guide says about currency
p: The Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) guide for passengers lists Indian and foreign currency above the prescribed limits as restricted goods. It says foreign currency above US$5,000 in notes, or US$10,000 or the equivalent in notes, banknotes and traveller's cheques together, must be declared on arrival.

For leaving India, the guide says export of Indian currency is strictly prohibited, except that Indian residents going abroad may take Indian notes up to Rs. 25,000. Tourists and NRIs may take out foreign currency up to the amount they brought in and declared on the Customs Declaration Form on arrival. Because no declaration is needed for up to US$5,000, the guide says tourists can generally take out up to that amount. Indian residents may take foreign currency without a limit if it was bought from an authorised foreign exchange dealer. The guide does not list penalties.
india.src: Source read: CBIC, Customs clearance of passengers at a glance (PDF). Penalties are not in it.

ireland.h: What Irish Revenue says about carrying cash
p: Irish Revenue says that if you enter or leave the EU at an Irish airport or port with EUR 10,000 or more, or the equivalent, you must make a declaration to Customs. Since 1 January 2021 the UK counts as outside the EU, so the rule covers moves to and from the UK, including the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands, but not to or from Northern Ireland. Cash covers banknotes and coins (including ones no longer in circulation but still exchangeable), cheques, traveller's cheques, promissory notes and money orders without a named payee, gold coins with at least 90% gold and gold bars, nuggets or clumps with at least 99.5% gold.

Separately from the declaration, a Customs officer may search for, seize and keep cash of EUR 1,000 or more entering or leaving the State if there are reasonable grounds to believe it is the proceeds of crime or meant for crime. You can ask Customs for a stamped copy of your completed declaration. Sending or receiving EUR 10,000 or more by post, freight or courier may require a disclosure declaration. The page we read does not describe the form, where to hand it in or the penalties.
ireland.src: Source read: Revenue (Ireland), Travelling with, or sending, cash. Form, submission steps and penalties are on other pages that we did not read.

italy.h: What the Italian Customs and Monopolies Agency says about cash
p: The Agenzia delle Dogane e dei Monopoli (ADM) traveller card of July 2025 says carrying cash or similar assets is free below EUR 10,000. From EUR 10,000 you must fill in a declaration, sign it and hand it in only at a customs office when entering or leaving Italy. The card says the rule applies to all movements to and from other EU countries and, in a separate section, to movements to and from non-EU countries. It names bearer negotiable instruments and highly liquid stores of value as covered.

Not declaring, or declaring wrongly or incompletely, is a breach of the currency rules. For an undeclared excess of up to EUR 10,000 the card sets administrative seizure of 50% of the excess and a fine of 30% to 50% of it. For an excess above EUR 10,000 and up to EUR 100,000 the seizure is 70% and the fine 50% to 70%. A wrong or incomplete declaration is charged on the difference between what you carried and what you declared, at lower percentages. The card also describes paying a reduced sum within 10 days of the breach, with a minimum of EUR 500 for an omitted declaration.
italy.src: Source read: ADM, Carta doganale del viaggiatore (July 2025). Percentages above EUR 100,000 and the postal rules were not summarised here.

indonesia.h: What the Travel Doc customs page says about cash in Indonesia
p: The Travel Doc customs page for Indonesia says funds of more than Rp100,000,000, or the equivalent in foreign currency, must be declared to customs.
The page names no publisher and shows no date, so confirm the figures with the customs authority before you travel.
indonesia.src: Unofficial source, read 16 November 2026: Travel Doc customs information page for Indonesia (infopages.traveldoc.aero, undated; it names no publisher). The official customs site could not be read.

israel.h: What the Travel Doc customs page says about cash in Israel
p: The Travel Doc customs page for Israel says funds of 50,000 shekels or more must be reported on entry (12,000 shekels from Gaza or across the Egypt and Jordan land borders), and 90,000 shekels or more on exit.
The page names no publisher and shows no date, so confirm the figures with the customs authority before you travel.
israel.src: Unofficial source, read 16 November 2026: Travel Doc customs information page for Israel (infopages.traveldoc.aero, undated; it names no publisher). The official customs site could not be read.

japan.h: What Japan Customs says about carrying means of payment
p: Japan Customs says you must declare cash and other means of payment worth more than 1 million yen when you enter or leave Japan. The lower threshold of 100,000 yen applies only to people leaving for North Korea. Cash includes foreign currency, and the rule also covers cheques, traveller's cheques, promissory notes and securities, and gold bullion of at least 90% purity weighing more than 1 kg.

You submit the form called Declaration of Carrying of Means of Payment, etc., and blank copies are available from a Customs officer at the airport or seaport. Gold is handled in two steps: you tick Yes for gold bullion or gold products on the baggage declaration whatever the amount, and if you carry more than 1 kg of gold at 90% purity or higher you also file the means-of-payment form. The page does not state penalties for failing to declare cash.
japan.src: Source read: Japan Customs, passenger page (English). Penalties for undeclared cash are not stated on it.

kenya.h: What the Kenya Revenue Authority says about declaring currency
p: The Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) passenger terminal page says currency of USD 10,000 or more, or its equivalent, must be declared when you arrive in Kenya. Arriving passengers make their declaration on the Passenger Declaration Form F88.

The same page warns that giving false information to a Customs officer is an offence under the East African Community Customs Management Act 2004, and that passengers who fail to declare or declare wrongly face strict penal action on conviction, with goods liable to seizure. That warning is written about goods, so the page does not make clear whether it applies to undeclared currency, and it says nothing about taking currency out of Kenya.
kenya.src: Source read: KRA, Passenger terminal clearance in Kenya. The page does not cover leaving Kenya or give a penalty for currency.

latvia.h: What the Latvian State Revenue Service says about cash
p: The Latvian State Revenue Service (VID) says that at crossings that are also the EU external border, each traveller entering or leaving Latvia must declare cash of EUR 10,000 or more, even when the cash belongs to someone else. Officials may also ask for a declaration from a traveller carrying less if there are signs of illegal activity. If you travel through another country, you declare at the first place where you cross the EU external border, so a flight from Turkey via Germany is declared in Germany. Cash covers banknotes and coins, blank cheques, traveller's cheques, promissory notes and money orders, coins with at least 90% gold and bullion with at least 99.5% gold.

At a two-channel crossing you go through the red channel and hand in the free declaration form, in Latvian or English, with a handwritten signature. It asks for the owner, the recipient, the origin and the intended use of the cash. Other currencies are converted at the ECB rate published on the penultimate Wednesday of the month.

Not declaring can bring an administrative fine of up to 20% of the amount, and the cash may be detained. Large amounts can lead to criminal liability, with up to three years in prison. For cash sent by post or courier, the sender or recipient files a disclosure declaration within 30 days of a request. The page does not describe movements across internal EU borders.
latvia.src: Source read: VID, Cash (English). Internal EU border rules are not on that page.

kuwait.h: Kuwait: what the UK government advice says
p: Our card repeats the UK government's travel advice for Kuwait, which we re-read today: you must declare cash or traveller's cheques worth 3,000 Kuwaiti dinars (about 7,500 pounds) or more, you are given a certified declaration proving you brought the money in, and without it your money could be seized when you leave Kuwait.

This is the advice of another country's government, not a Kuwaiti authority, which is why the card is marked unofficial. The page does not say which Kuwaiti body issues the certificate, how the declaration is made or what the penalty is, so ask Kuwaiti customs or your airline before you carry a large amount.
kuwait.src: Source read: UK government (FCDO), Kuwait entry requirements. This is an unofficial source for Kuwait.

jamaica.h: Cash in Jamaica: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says the Customs passenger declaration, form C5, asks whether you are carrying currency or monetary instruments worth more than US$10,000 or the equivalent. On the Jamaica Customs Agency passenger page we read today, all arriving passengers must complete the electronic C5 declaration, in force since 1 September 2023, free of charge for visitors and residents.

We could not re-open the official page, so we checked the UK government's travel advice for Jamaica, an unofficial source. On cash it says to declare cash or travellers' cheques of 10,000 US dollars or more on the C5 form, to complete the Financial Investigation Division cross-border form, and to give proof of where the money comes from and what it is for. In practice, a traveller who carries more than the threshold fills in a short form at the border, shows the money if asked, and gets a stamped copy to prove it was declared. Jamaica's threshold is on the card; the Jamaica Customs Agency holds the form.
jamaica.src: UK government (FCDO) entry requirements page, read 16 November 2026. It is an unofficial source: it is another country's travel advice.

jordan.h: Cash in Jordan: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says that if you carry cash or bearer negotiable instruments worth more than JOD 10,000, or the equivalent, you must declare them, and it cites article 23-A of Jordan's Anti-Money Laundering and Counter Terrorist Financing Law No. 20 of 2021. That comes from the guide of Queen Alia International Airport, which is why the card is marked unofficial.

The official page could not be re-opened, and the UK government's travel advice for Jordan, which we also read, says nothing about cash. So this section applies the general rule most countries follow: in practice, a traveller who carries more than the threshold fills in a short form at the border, shows the money if asked, and gets a stamped copy to prove it was declared. Jordan's threshold is on the card; Jordan Customs holds the form.
jordan.src: Official page not re-opened; the UK government (FCDO) advice read on 16 November 2026 does not cover cash. Global rule applied, unofficial.

luxembourg.h: What Luxembourg Customs says about cross-border cash
p: The Luxembourg customs and excise administration says any movement of cash worth EUR 10,000 or more across a border to or from Luxembourg must be declared, whether you carry it or send it. It counts cash and bearer negotiable instruments, and since the EU rules changed it also counts gold coins (90% gold) and unminted gold (99.5% gold) above that value. Jewellery and diamonds are not cash in law, but they need a separate customs declaration.

The declaration is made before the trip or when you cross the border. The notice says to file it electronically beforehand, and if you have not, to go to customs yourself, for example at Findel airport. Cash sent by express courier, post or freight needs a disclosure declaration. Breaking these duties is punished by a fine of EUR 251 to EUR 25,000, which can come with partial confiscation of the money. The notice cites EU Regulation 2018/1672, in force since 3 June 2021, and the Luxembourg law of 16 July 2021.
luxembourg.src: Source read: Douanes Luxembourg, news notice on cross-border cash movements (in French, from 2020). The Guichet.lu page and the form steps were not readable.

maldives.h: What the Maldives regulation says about carrying cash
p: Regulation 2015/R-111 on the cross-border cash declaration amount, in an unofficial English translation on the Maldives Monetary Authority site, says any person who enters or leaves the Maldives carrying cash of US$10,000 or more, or the equivalent in rufiyaa or another currency, must report it to the Maldives Customs Service. The regulation took effect on 22 March 2015 and was amended for the second time on 17 January 2021. It is made under section 24(a) of the Prevention of Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism Act, Law No. 10/2014.

That is all the two-page file says. It does not set out the form, the penalty or how the report is made, and the Customs regulation our card also links did not open for us today, so we cannot re-check what it says about the online application or about declaring before the airline gives a boarding pass. Check Maldives Customs before you travel.
maldives.src: Source read: Maldives Monetary Authority, Regulation on Cross Border Cash Declaration Amount (unofficial English translation). Form, penalty and the Customs regulation were not re-read.

lithuania.h: What Lithuanian Customs says about cash
p: Lithuanian Customs says anyone entering Lithuania from a third country, or leaving it for one, with EUR 10,000 or more (or the equivalent) must hand in the Cash Declaration Form at the customs office at the border point without being asked. At an airport use the red channel, not the green one. If the cash is in your hold bag, declare it before you check the bag in. Allow enough time, and on trains the form is handed to the customs officers on board.

Cash means notes and coins, cheques, traveller's cheques, promissory notes and money orders, and also gold coins of at least 90% and gold bars or nuggets of at least 99.5%. Several currencies are added together at the Bank of Lithuania rate of that day. The person carrying the money declares it, whoever owns it: a father carrying EUR 30,000 that belongs to the whole family files the form himself.

Between Lithuania and another EU country, you declare more than EUR 10,000 when a customs officer asks, and an officer may ask for a lower sum if money laundering or other offences are suspected. Customs also asks for copies of documents showing where the cash comes from, such as a bank statement, an inheritance document, a sale contract or lottery winnings. A false, incomplete or missing declaration can bring a fine and detention of the cash under the Code of Administrative Offences.
lithuania.src: Official source read 23 November 2026: Lithuanian Customs (Lietuvos Respublikos muitine), "Cash declaration" page (muitine.lrv.lt, English; read from an archived copy because the live site refuses our reader).

malta.h: What the Maltese tax and customs administration says about cash
p: The Malta Tax and Customs Administration says that anyone entering, leaving or passing through Malta with EUR 10,000 or more in cash, or the equivalent in other currencies, must declare it to customs under subsidiary legislation 233.07. Unaccompanied cash of the same value entering, leaving or passing through Malta must be declared by the sender, the recipient or a representative within 30 days of the Commissioner asking for a disclosure declaration.

Cash is wider than banknotes. The page, citing Article 2 of Regulation (EU) 2018/1672, counts currency, bearer-negotiable instruments, commodities used as highly liquid stores of value (such as gold) and prepaid cards. You declare on the EU Cash Declaration Form, with a separate non-EU form and additional sheets available. The page states no penalty.
malta.src: Source read on 22 November 2026: Malta Tax and Customs Administration (mtca.gov.mt), Information to Travellers on Cash Declaration.

malaysia.h: Cash in Malaysia: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says to declare cash, traveller's cheques and other bearer negotiable instruments worth more than US$10,000 when you arrive or leave, that Malaysian ringgit above that value may not go in or out without written approval from Bank Negara Malaysia, and that not declaring is an offence. It comes from the Customs form we link below the card.

We could not re-open the official page, so we checked the UK government's travel advice for Malaysia, an unofficial source. On cash it says to declare cash or travellers' cheques of 10,000 US dollars or more, to get approval before moving that much in ringgit, and warns of a fine of up to 3 million ringgit and up to 5 years in prison. Carrying money across a border is never banned by itself, but a large amount without a declaration is the single most common reason cash is seized. For Malaysia, the figure on the card is what to follow, and the Royal Malaysian Customs Department can confirm it.
malaysia.src: UK government (FCDO) entry requirements page, read 16 November 2026. It is an unofficial source: it is another country's travel advice.

lebanon.h: What Lebanese Customs says about cash
p: The Lebanese Customs traveller's guide says that anyone physically carrying cash, cheques, promissory notes, payment orders, bearer shares or prepaid payment cards must declare them to customs when the value is above 15,000 US dollars or the equivalent in another currency. This rests on Law 42 of 24 November 2015, and the traveller fills in a declaration form giving full details.

The threshold applies to people entering and to people leaving Lebanon. It is higher than the 10,000 euro or dollar figure used in the EU and in many other countries, so do not assume 10,000 applies here.
lebanon.src: Official source read 23 November 2026: Lebanese Customs Administration, "Traveller's guide" (customs.gov.lb, in Arabic, translated by us; copyright 2019 on the site).

netherlands.h: What Dutch Customs (Douane) says about cash and gold
p: Dutch Customs says you must always declare cash or gold worth EUR 10,000 or more when you enter or leave the EU. The page covers people travelling by plane, boat or car, and ship crews and passengers, who can declare themselves or through a shipping agent. For a trip that crosses the EU border indirectly, you declare at the point where you cross it, so a journey from Istanbul to Rotterdam is declared on entry in Greece or Bulgaria.

Leaving the Netherlands by air for a non-EU country, you declare at the tax refund office in departure hall 3 at Schiphol, before you check in your luggage and go through security. At other airports you declare at Customs at the airport. Arriving from outside the EU, you use the exit marked Goods to declare. By ship you hand the cash declaration form to the Customs Office of the port, or an agent emails it beforehand. The page does not describe penalties or travel inside the EU.
netherlands.src: Source read: douane.nl, Entering or leaving the EU with 10,000 euro or more (English). Penalties and intra-EU travel are not on that page.

new-zealand.h: What New Zealand Customs says about the Border Cash Report
p: New Zealand Customs says you must complete a Border Cash Report if you carry NZ$10,000 or more in cash, or the foreign equivalent, into or out of New Zealand. Under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009, cash means physical currency and bearer-negotiable instruments such as a bill of exchange, cheque, promissory note, bearer bond, traveller's cheque or money order. The Act does not ban moving cash, it requires the report, and the same duty covers a person who is to receive unaccompanied cash of that amount sent from abroad.

You can use the online form only within 72 hours of travel, or the printable form NZCS 337. The Customs fact sheet says the completed forms go to the Police Commissioner. Failing to report is an offence: for an individual up to three months in prison or a fine of up to NZ$10,000, or both, and for a company a fine of up to NZ$50,000. That fact sheet carries an issue date of October 2018, so check the amounts with Customs.
new-zealand.src: Source read: New Zealand Customs, Leaving New Zealand page and Fact Sheet 13 (issued October 2018).

nepal.h: What the Nepal aeronautical information publication says about cash
p: Nepal's official aeronautical information publication, issued by the Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, includes a passenger customs section. It says no customs formalities are normally required for departing passengers, but restrictions on carrying foreign currency in and out of the country remain in force. A passenger who brings or takes more than five thousand US dollars in cash must declare it at the Customs Office, as the Customs Department prescribes.

The same section says exports of antiques and precious or semi-precious stones need clearance and a certificate from the Department of Archaeology. The publication is an aviation document, not a page of the Customs Department, and it does not give the form, the rupee rules or any penalty. Check with Nepal Customs before you carry a large amount.
nepal.src: Source read: Civil Aviation Authority of Nepal, AIP Nepal (customs section). It is an aviation publication and does not cover penalties.

mauritius.h: What the Travel Doc customs page says about cash in Mauritius
p: The Travel Doc customs page for Mauritius says currency of more than Rs500,000 must be declared to customs.
The page names no publisher and shows no date, so confirm the figures with the customs authority before you travel.
mauritius.src: Unofficial source, read 16 November 2026: Travel Doc customs information page for Mauritius (infopages.traveldoc.aero, undated; it names no publisher). The official customs site could not be read.

mexico.h: What the Travel Doc customs page says about cash in Mexico
p: The Travel Doc customs page for Mexico says currency of more than US$10,000 must be declared to customs. It gives no separate threshold for other forms of cash.
The page names no publisher and shows no date, so confirm the figures with the customs authority before you travel.
mexico.src: Unofficial source, read 16 November 2026: Travel Doc customs information page for Mexico (infopages.traveldoc.aero, undated; it names no publisher). The official customs site could not be read.

morocco.h: Cash in Morocco: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says to declare foreign cash or payment instruments worth 100,000 dirhams or more at the entry customs office, that you can also declare smaller amounts, and that the endorsed declaration is valid for one stay, up to six months for non-residents, and proves where the money came from when you leave. It comes from the Moroccan customs page we link below the card.

We could not re-open the official page, so we checked the UK government's travel advice for Morocco, an unofficial source. On cash it says to declare foreign currency worth 100,000 dirham or more on entry or exit, and adds that the dirham is not convertible outside Morocco. Whatever the threshold, the safe habit is to declare when you are close to it, keep the receipt or stamped form, and be ready to say where the money comes from. Moroccan Customs sets the rule for Morocco.
morocco.src: UK government (FCDO) entry requirements page, read 16 November 2026. It is an unofficial source: it is another country's travel advice.

norway.h: What Norwegian Customs says about carrying currency
p: Norwegian Customs says you must declare currency worth more than NOK 25,000 when you bring it into or out of Norway, and that no tax is charged on it. It counts Norwegian and foreign notes and coins and other means of payment, such as gift cards. You complete the form Declaration of cash and cash equivalents and hand in two copies, at the customs office you leave from, such as at the airport, or in the red channel when you arrive.

Not declaring brings a fine of 20% of the whole amount, not only the part above NOK 25,000, so NOK 26,000 unreported means a fine of NOK 5,200. Customs may instead report the case to the police, and if it suspects the money is linked to crime it confiscates all of it while the case is investigated. People who send or receive money through banks or payment companies do not report it, because those institutions report to the Currency Register. The page does not mention EU rules.

oman.h: What Oman Customs says about carrying currency
p: Oman's General Directorate of Customs says travellers arriving or leaving with currency, bearer securities, banknotes, or precious metals and gemstones that can be turned into cash, above the threshold of OMR 6,000 or the equivalent, must declare them on the currency declaration form linked from the page. The page words the threshold in two ways, as 6,000 riyals and as 6,000 or more, so a traveller with exactly OMR 6,000 should declare to be safe.

The page says a verbal, written or electronic declaration, or simply going through the green or red channel, counts as declaring the goods you carry, but it does not say which channel to use for currency. It lists no fines for undeclared currency. It states only that not declaring cash, traveller's cheques or precious metals is illegal under Article 53 of the Money Laundering and Terrorism Financing Law.
oman.src: Source read: Oman Customs, Traveller services. No fine for undeclared currency is stated on the page.

peru.h: What SUNAT says about cash in baggage
p: The Peruvian customs authority SUNAT lists cash and negotiable financial instruments, in US dollars or an equivalent currency, as exempt baggage up to and including US$10,000, which means no Sworn Baggage Declaration is needed for that amount. The page does not say in so many words that amounts above US$10,000 must be declared.

Its penalty notice does refer to declaring money: if a traveller omits or misstates cash or negotiable instruments, customs temporarily retains the money and applies a penalty of 30% of the undeclared value, under Law No. 28306 and its amendments. For the exact form to use above US$10,000, ask SUNAT before you travel.
peru.src: Source read: SUNAT, Equipaje y bienes (viajeros). The form for amounts above US$10,000 is not on that page.

panama.h: Panama: what Tourism Panama says about declaring cash
p: We re-read the Tourism Panama travel requirements page. It says you only need to declare at customs if you carry cash, objects or documents worth more than US$10,000, in which case you complete the online traveller's affidavit, get a QR code and show it at customs. If you have nothing to declare, you fill in no forms, including the affidavit.

Tourism Panama is the tourism authority, not the customs authority, which is why the card is marked unofficial. The page gives no penalty and does not describe the rules for leaving Panama, so ask Panamanian customs before you carry a large amount.
panama.src: Source read: Tourism Panama, Travel requirements. This is an unofficial source for customs rules.

nigeria.h: Cash in Nigeria: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says a Nigeria Customs Service notice from 2016 asks passengers carrying cash above US$10,000 for information, and calls this the position of the law. We tried to open that notice again today and the site refused the request, so we could not re-read it or check whether the threshold has changed since 2016.

The official page could not be re-opened, and the UK government's travel advice for Nigeria, which we also read, says nothing about cash. So this section applies the general rule most countries follow: carrying money across a border is never banned by itself, but a large amount without a declaration is the single most common reason cash is seized. For Nigeria, the figure on the card is what to follow, and the Nigeria Customs Service can confirm it.
nigeria.src: Official page not re-opened; the UK government (FCDO) advice read on 16 November 2026 does not cover cash. Global rule applied, unofficial.

philippines.h: Cash in Philippines: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says to declare foreign currency above US$10,000, or the equivalent in another currency, on the Customs Baggage Declaration Form. It comes from the foreign currency page of the Bureau of Customs that we link below the card.

We could not re-open the official page, so we checked the UK government's travel advice for Philippines, an unofficial source. On cash it says that you cannot bring in more than 50,000 pesos and must declare foreign cash or cheques worth more than 10,000 US dollars on a form on arrival. Border cash rules follow one common idea: you may bring money, but large sums must be declared, and a missing declaration can cost you the money. Check the Bureau of Customs for the current Philippines threshold and the form.
philippines.src: UK government (FCDO) entry requirements page, read 16 November 2026. It is an unofficial source: it is another country's travel advice.

qatar.h: What Qatar Customs says about cash, metals and stones
p: Qatar Customs says travellers must declare cash, precious metals or stones, or negotiable bearer instruments worth QAR 50,000 or more, or the equivalent in foreign currency, when they enter or leave the country. Cash means Qatari riyals or foreign currency. Bearer instruments are documents payable to whoever holds them, such as traveller's cheques, cheques, promissory notes and payment orders. Precious metals include gold, silver and platinum, and precious stones include diamonds, emeralds, rubies, sapphires and pearls. The introduction speaks of precious jewellery while the detailed rules speak of metals and stones, so ask Customs how jewellery is treated.

You fill in the Customs Declaration Form at the customs declaration office at air, sea and land outlets and give any extra information the officer asks for. Failing to declare, giving false information or refusing to explain the source of the funds can mean up to three years in prison, a fine of QAR 100,000 to QAR 500,000 or twice the value of the funds, whichever is greater, and confiscation. The page names Anti-Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Law No. 20 of 2019 as the legal basis.
qatar.src: Source read: Qatar General Authority of Customs, travellers exemptions page (English).

portugal.h: What the Portuguese Tax and Customs Authority says about cash
p: The Portuguese Tax and Customs Authority (AT) says that if you enter or leave the EU through a Portuguese airport or port with EUR 10,000 or more in cash, you must declare it to Customs. Cash covers banknotes and coins, including ones no longer in general circulation but still exchangeable, cheques, traveller's cheques, promissory notes and payment orders without a named payee, gold coins with at least 90% gold and gold bars, nuggets or clumps with at least 99.5% gold. Gold has been included since 3 June 2021.

You declare through the customs portal application or with the form Declaração de Dinheiro Líquido under Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2018/1672. For unaccompanied cash of EUR 10,000 or more sent by post, cargo or express service, a disclosure declaration under Article 4 is required only if Customs asks. Customs can always check the declaration and the cash, and you can ask for a certified copy of your declaration. The page we read does not mention penalties.
portugal.src: Source read: Autoridade Tributária e Aduaneira, Viaja com dinheiro líquido? (in Portuguese). Penalties are not on that page.

poland.h: What LOT Polish Airlines says about cash on flights from Poland
p: LOT's help page says that between Schengen countries you do not need to declare cash, even above 10,000 euros. If your trip crosses the Schengen border, amounts of 10,000 euros or more must be declared to the customs authority.

For flights to or from the USA, LOT gives US$10,000 as the limit for funds you can carry without declaring. It lists what counts as declarable: banknotes and coins in Polish or foreign currency, withdrawn coins of value, securities, cheques, bills of exchange and precious metals such as gold or silver coins and bars.

LOT adds that these limits apply to every way of crossing a border, not only flying, and points to official government sites for current limits. The airline page is not the customs authority's, so confirm with Polish customs.
poland.src: Unofficial source, read 22 November 2026: LOT Polish Airlines help page "How much cash can you travel with?". It is an airline page, not the customs authority's.
link: LOT Polish Airlines: How much cash can you travel with?

romania.h: What TAROM tells passengers about cash in Romania
p: TAROM, Romania's national airline, tells passengers entering or leaving Romania to include cash above 10,000 euros, or the equivalent in another currency, in their customs statement. The same list names weapons and explosives, medicines and chemicals, jewels beyond personal needs, and art objects that belong to the state heritage.

That matches the EU rule on our card: declare EUR 10,000 or more when entering or leaving the EU. The airline page is not the customs authority, so confirm the form and the corridor with Romanian customs.
romania.src: Unofficial source, read 22 November 2026: TAROM, the Romanian national airline, page "Customs clearance". It is not the customs authority's page, whose site could not be read.

russia.h: Cash in Russia: the card, an unofficial source and the general rule
p: Our card says cash and traveller's cheques must be declared when the total you bring in or take out at one time is more than the equivalent of US$10,000, that other monetary instruments must be declared whatever the amount, and that above US$100,000 you must also hand over documents that show where the money comes from. It comes from the Russian customs page we link below the card.

We could not re-open the official page, so we checked the UK government's travel advice for Russia, an unofficial source. On cash it says that you can bring in up to 10,000 US dollars without declaring and cannot leave with more than 10,000 US dollars even with a declaration, with fines, confiscation or prosecution for breaking customs rules. Carrying money across a border is never banned by itself, but a large amount without a declaration is the single most common reason cash is seized. For Russia, the figure on the card is what to follow, and the Russian Federal Customs Service can confirm it.
russia.src: UK government (FCDO) entry requirements page, read 16 November 2026. It is an unofficial source: it is another country's travel advice.

saudi-arabia.h: What the Travel Doc customs page says about cash in Saudi Arabia
p: The Travel Doc customs page for Saudi Arabia says any amount of currency may be imported, but amounts above SAR 60,000 (or the foreign equivalent) must be declared.
The page names no publisher and shows no date, so confirm the figures with the customs authority before you travel.
saudi-arabia.src: Unofficial source, read 16 November 2026: Travel Doc customs information page for Saudi Arabia (infopages.traveldoc.aero, undated; it names no publisher). The official customs site could not be read.
link: Travel Doc: Saudi Arabia customs information

serbia.h: What Serbian Customs says about cash
p: The Serbian customs administration says you must declare cash of EUR 10,000 or more, in dinars or any other currency, to Customs, with no limit on how much you may bring in. The threshold applies to each person, including children, and payment cards can be carried freely. You ask the customs officer for a Cash Declaration Form at the entry or exit point and should keep the certified copy.

Everyone may take out up to EUR 10,000 without documents. A non-resident who wants to take out more needs one of three receipts, each covering up to the amount on it: the certified Cash Declaration Form from entry, a Serbian bank receipt for a withdrawal from their own account, or an exchange office receipt for dinars obtained with payment cards in Serbia. Customs cancels these receipts the first time you leave Serbia, even for a short trip to a neighbouring country, so you need a new certified form when you come back or pass through. Residents may take out more only with evidence of how it came in. The page lists no fines. It warns that without a certified form the cash over EUR 10,000 risks seizure when you leave.
serbia.src: Source read: Carina.rs, FAQ for tourists (English). Fines are not on the page.

seychelles.h: What Seychelles Revenue Commission says about cash
p: The Seychelles Revenue Commission says visitors and residents carrying cash of SCR 50,000 or more, or the foreign equivalent, must declare it when entering and leaving. On arrival you answer yes or no to the currency question on the Seychelles Electronic Border System. If you answer yes, you go to the red customs channel, complete the Cash Declaration Form and give proof of the source of the funds.

On departure you go to the customs office at the VAT verification counter at Seychelles International Airport, where an officer has you complete the form and checks the amount and your proof; if the counter is empty, you call an officer from the phone there. Failing to declare, or making a false or misleading declaration, is an offence with a fine under section 75(2) of the Act, and customs may seize undeclared amounts above SCR 50,000 under the AMLCFT Act 2020. The page does not state the fine.
seychelles.src: Source read: Seychelles Revenue Commission, Customs and Excises. The fine amount is not on the page.

singapore.h: What the Singapore Police say about reporting cash
p: The Singapore Police Force Suspicious Transaction Reporting Office says you must report physical currency and bearer negotiable instruments above S$20,000, or the equivalent, moved into or out of Singapore. This covers coins and banknotes and instruments such as traveller's cheques, bills of exchange, promissory notes, bearer bonds, money orders and postal orders. The page stresses that there is no limit on how much you may move, only a duty to report.

Travellers use Form NP 727, submitted online within 72 hours before they enter or leave, through the ICA website, the MyICA app, or after the Singapore Arrival Card. Senders, carriers and recipients of cash sent by cargo or post use Form NP 728, which must reach the office at least one business day before the move, or within five business days of receipt for a recipient. Failing to give a full and accurate report is an offence with a fine of up to S$50,000, up to three years in prison, or both, and the cash may be seized.
singapore.src: Source read: Singapore Police Force, Cross-border cash movement reporting.

south-africa.h: What SARS says about excess currency
p: The South African Revenue Service policy on excess currency, effective 1 July 2026, applies to anyone entering or leaving from or to a country outside the Common Monetary Area with rand banknotes, foreign currency or Kruger Rand coins. On arrival you declare South African banknotes, and on departure you declare South African banknotes, securities and gold, on the traveller card TD-01 or the electronic traveller declaration. Visitors in air transit do not have to declare, but once your passport is stamped as entered you are no longer in transit.

Customs officers may search for and seize currency when a traveller has more than R100,000 in rand notes, when foreign currency is more than the amount a non-resident declared on arrival, or when there is no permission from the National Treasury. Seized currency is forfeited to the National Revenue Fund, though the Treasury may return it, in whole or in part. Up to 15 Kruger Rand coins may be taken out if they were bought with foreign currency brought in. Separately, cash above R100,000 must be reported under the Financial Intelligence Centre Act, and linked smaller amounts can be added together.
south-africa.src: Source read: SARS, SC-PA-01-06 Excess Currency External Policy (revision 11, effective 1 July 2026).

slovakia.h: What the Slovak Financial Administration says about cash
p: The Slovak Financial Administration says every person carrying cash of EUR 10,000 or more, or the equivalent in another currency, into, out of or through Slovakia must give written notice to the border customs office without being asked, under paragraph 4 of the Customs Act. There are two forms: Form 1a for cash that travels with you and Form 2a for cash sent without a person. Cash is not only currency, and the page also covers cash sent by post, freight or courier.

Failing to declare, with or without an accompanying person, is a customs offence for individuals, and for businesses it is a delict under paragraph 72(1)(n) of Act No. 199/2004. The page we read did not state a fine. The page is long, and we read only its first part.
slovakia.src: Source read: Finančná správa, Zákazy a obmedzenia (in Slovak), first 100,000 characters. Fines are not stated in the part read.

slovenia.h: What the Slovenian Financial Administration says about cross-border cash
p: The Financial Administration of Slovenia (FURS) guidance on cross-border cash says cash of EUR 10,000 or more, or the equivalent, must be declared when you cross the EU external border. It counts banknotes, coins, cheques, traveller's cheques, promissory notes and payment orders without a named payee, gold coins with at least 90% gold and gold bars or bullion with at least 99.5% gold. The guidance cites EU Regulation 2018/1672 and Slovenia's anti-money-laundering law (ZPPDFT-2).

You use the official cash declaration form, available on the website or at border control points. For movements between Slovenia and another EU country, no declaration is needed unless customs or the police ask for one. For cash sent without a traveller, customs may require a declaration, which the sender, recipient or representative submits within 30 days of the request. The authorities may detain the cash and penalise you for not complying, but the document gives no fine.
slovenia.src: Source read: FURS, Čezmejni prenosi gotovine (description document, in Slovenian). Fine amounts are not stated in it.

south-korea.h: What Korea Customs says about means of payment
p: The Korea Customs Service page on goods to be declared lists means of payment, etc., exceeding US$10,000 among the items travellers must report to Customs, and ties the threshold to the Foreign Exchange Transactions Regulations, citing specific articles.

That is all the page says on money. It does not explain what counts as a means of payment, how or when to report, or what the penalty is, and the tax penalties it lists apply to goods above the tax-free allowance, not to money. Check Korea Customs or the Bank of Korea before you carry a large amount.
south-korea.src: Source read: Korea Customs Service, goods to be declared page (English). Method, scope and penalties are not on the page.

spain.h: What the Spanish Tax Agency says about declaring cash
p: The Spanish Tax Agency (AEAT) says you must declare any amount of EUR 10,000 or more, or the equivalent in any currency, per person and trip. The page names four forms: E1 for accompanied cash to or from a non-EU country, E2 for unaccompanied cash to or from a non-EU country, S1 for accompanied cash within Spain or to or from another EU country, and S2 for unaccompanied cash in those cases. One declaration covers all your means of payment together. Movements within Spain are declared from EUR 100,000.

You declare before the movement; unaccompanied cash can be declared up to 30 days before. Cash includes banknotes and coins, traveller's cheques and certain cheques or payment orders, prepaid cards not linked to a bank account, gold coins of at least 90% and bullion of at least 99.5%. Bank transfers are not declared, whatever the amount. A parent or guardian declares for a minor. Not declaring is a serious infraction with a fine of at least EUR 600 and up to 50% of the value of the cash, and the cash can be provisionally seized if the declaration is missing, wrong or incomplete or there are signs of crime.
spain.src: Source read: Agencia Tributaria, Medios de pago (Spanish).

sri-lanka.h: What Sri Lanka Customs says about currency
p: Sri Lanka Customs says you may carry any amount of currency as long as it was legally acquired. Bringing in more than US$15,000, or the equivalent, must be declared, and Customs issues a currency declaration receipt. Taking out more than US$10,000, or the equivalent, must be declared. If you want to take previously declared money back out, declare it even if it is under US$15,000.

The page speaks of the equivalent in other currencies only, so it says nothing separate about Sri Lankan rupees. It lists no penalties. Check Sri Lanka Customs or the Central Bank before you carry a large amount.
sri-lanka.src: Source read: Sri Lanka Customs, Passenger Services Directorate. Penalties and rupee rules are not on the page.
